What next for Wales after another winless Six Nations?

Wales duo Lewis and Jones depart Gloucester-Hartpury

Lynn's side ended a nine-game losing streak against Barbarians at Allianz Stadium.

They lost all five of their Six Nations matches for the second year in a row, finishing bottom for a third consecutive season.

The extended squad features 37 players who have played Celtic Challenge rugby for Brython Thunder and Gwalia Lightning and includes new faces in fly half Ffion Williams, prop Crystal James and hooker Shannelle Williams, while centre Savannah Picton Powell returns after injury.

"All the players were given individualised training programmes which they followed before meeting up for block one of pre-season," added Lynn.

title: Scotland and Dutch boards criticise ICC for World Cup changes
description: The cricket boards of Scotland and the Netherlands criticise the International Cricket Council for structural changes made to men's 50-over World Cup.
fullText:
The cricket boards of Scotland and the Netherlands have criticised the International Cricket Council for structural changes made to the men's 50-over World Cup.

Last month the ICC announced the main part of the tournament for 2027 would be 12 teams in two groups of six, rather than 14 as originally planned.

The three lowest-ranked qualifiers will instead be placed in a preliminary three-team Super Series, from which only the winner will progress.

It effectively means the likes of Scotland and the Netherlands face three qualifying tournaments to reach the main group stage of the World Cup.

A joint statement from Cricket Scotland and Royal Dutch Association (KNCB) said they had "significant concerns" about the "impact of these changes" along with the "process through which they have been introduced".

"The changes risk weakening the integrity and credibility of international cricket, and only highlights the importance of strong governance, transparent decision-making and effective engagement with members," the statement said.

"Changing those structures at short notice creates significant uncertainty, disrupts planning, and places additional operational and financial pressure on organisations that are already operating with limited resources."

BBC Sport has approached the ICC for comment.

ICC considers World Cup cuts & WTC semis in overhaul

Scotland scrape past UAE with one wicket & ball left

The changes to the World Cup were agreed during meetings at the ICC's annual conference held in Edinburgh in June.

However, BBC Sport understands nearly all associate members were kept in the dark over the changes despite being present at the conference.

Cricket Scotland and the KNCB said they remain "fully committed" to "working constructively with the ICC".

But the two boards accused the global governing body of being "disrespectful" in how they have handled some of the discussions following the announcement.

"Cricket Scotland, KNCB and other associate members met twice with the ICC, seeking official written communication on the changes and greater clarity around the processes involved," the statement added.

"We also requested positive action to strengthen future operational decision-making and an invitation to bilateral planning meetings with full members.

"Since the second meeting more than two weeks ago, there has been no further response from the ICC, which is disappointing and disrespectful given the significance of the issues raised."

The joint statement follows concerns raised by the World Cricketers' Association last month over the decision.

Scotland and the Netherlands are the two highest ranked associate members.

Their decision to issue such a pointed statement reflects frustrations outside of full members with aspects of ICC decision making.

BBC Sport understands proposals were tabled at the 2025 ICC annual conference to create a single-class of membership, rather than having associate and full members, but it did progress.

The statement added that the changes to the World Cup qualifying were a "setback" for associate members and "risk undermining the progress made in recent years to grow the global game".

"At a time when cricket is seeking to expand its reach, attract new audiences and strengthen its position on the international sporting landscape, reducing meaningful opportunities for emerging nations sends entirely the wrong message," it said.

The statement also called on the ICC to "re-engage with associate members" and to do so "openly" to enable the sport to develop outside of full members.

"Leaders in cricket have consistently spoken about their ambition for the sport to become truly global," added the statement.

"Providing meaningful opportunities for emerging nations to qualify for, and compete at, major events is fundamental to achieving that ambition.

"Decisions that reduce or limit those opportunities slow the progress being made to expand the game's reach and appeal and runs counter to those ambitions."

title: 'I've cried non-stop' - Ditcheva breaks both hands again
description: Dakota Ditcheva says she broke both of her hands during the win over Denise Kielholtz - months after recovering from similar injuries.
fullText:
Dakota Ditcheva says she has "cried non-stop" after breaking both of her hands in the win over Denise Kielholtz - just months after recovering from similar injuries.

The Briton outclassed Kielholtz at PFL New York earlier this month to win by unanimous decision in her first fight in just over a year.

The 28-year-old had not fought since July 2025 as a result of breaking her left hand - then suffered a fracture in her other hand five months later.

Despite comfortably beating Kielholtz on her return, Ditcheva says she fought the majority of the contest with two broken hands.

"I broke my hands in the fight. I could feel it from the second I started the second round," she said on YouTube., external

"I didn't tell my corner. I didn't tell anybody. I didn't show it this time, and I didn't actually tell anybody until I got out of the cage.

"I am back in splints until my surgeon has decided what the next steps are going forward, which will be in the next few days."

Ditcheva, who extended the unbeaten start to her career to 16 fights, said one of her injuries occurred after opting not to have surgery on it last year while the other is a "small break on the other finger that didn't hold up so well".

"The good thing is I have no new breaks. It's just the hand that wasn't operated on that I broke at the end of last year," added Ditcheva.

"I was told that if I didn't go ahead with surgery at that time, there was a possibility it could break again. I took the risk in not doing the surgery because I was hoping it would hold strong, and it didn't.

"So therefore I'm paying the price for it now and I will be out for a little bit."

The injuries are another setback for Ditcheva, one of the biggest stars in the PFL and one of Britain's most talented fighters.

She won the PFL's flyweight tournament in 2024 to become the first British woman to claim a major MMA world championship, while securing a $1m (£787,000) prize.

Ditcheva is confident her lay-off will not last as long as her previous time on the sidelines.

"I have honestly cried non-stop the last week," she said.

"I will be back. This is not going to take me out. My career is not done.

"Although it felt like that once again, I will be back. I'm hopefully going to be back quicker than I was last time."

title: Championship all-stars to global gamble – will Ipswich's approach work?
description: As Ipswich prepare for their return to the Premier League, BBC Sport look at how they are approaching the transfer market differently.
fullText:
Newly promoted Ipswich Town have quietly been the Premier League's fourth-biggest net spenders so far this summer, behind only Chelsea, Tottenham and Arsenal.

Ten players have joined for a combined £106.6m, but what is most notable about the Tractor Boys' approach under new manager Gary O'Neil is the sea change in recruitment strategy, shaped by lessons learned from their chastening single season in the top flight in 2024-25.

Under O'Neil's popular predecessor Kieran McKenna, who stepped down on 10 June after overseeing three promotions in four full seasons, the Blues targeted players familiar with English football.

McKenna's success was built mainly on players from the UK and Republic of Ireland, supplemented by a handful of overseas additions already accustomed to the language and culture through spells at other English clubs.

Ipswich made 39 permanent first-team signings during McKenna's four-and-a-half-year reign, 32 of them either born or raised in Britain or Ireland, with just two joining directly from European clubs.

But the premium on domestic talent makes it difficult, if not impossible, to bridge the gulf between the Championship and Premier League. The success of Sunderland and Leeds last season demonstrated that for promoted teams to thrive, finding value in the transfer market is essential.

When Ipswich last went up in 2024, 10 of their 12 summer signings were British or Irish players acquired from other English sides.

This time, the Blues have cast their net far wider, with Emersonn and Florentino Luis set to be the first Brazilians to represent the club, Sasa Lukic the first Serbian and Daizen Maeda the first Japanese player.

Of the 10 players purchased, the only Briton is Chuba Akpom from Ajax. Even his arrival is an anomaly, given Ipswich were obliged to buy him following promotion despite an underwhelming loan spell.

New boss O'Neil aims to keep Ipswich in top flight

A youngster to watch at each Premier League club this season

Ipswich's previous recruitment model can be traced back to their four seasons in League One.

After guiding Town back to the Championship in 2023, McKenna admitted the club had made a "conscious decision" not to target overseas players because of the fast and frantic nature of England's third tier.

A largely unchanged – but tightly knit – squad then exceeded expectations by finishing second in the Championship in 2023-24, making Ipswich the first side in 12 years to reach the Premier League through back-to-back promotions.

At that point, the Blues' hierarchy could have ripped up the modus operandi that had served them so well and pivoted towards more extensive overseas recruitment. Instead, they doubled down on the approach, focusing mainly on emerging domestic talent largely unproven beyond the Championship.

A £100m summer spending spree brought Omari Hutchinson, Jack Clarke, Liam Delap, Dara O'Shea and Jacob Greaves to Portman Road – players who had primarily shone in the second tier but were identified as having the potential to develop into established Premier League performers.

Mindful that the odds were against survival, Ipswich also targeted players thought unlikely to baulk at remaining part of the project in the event of relegation.

McKenna's 'Championship all-stars' fell well short of safety, finishing second bottom with just 22 points, 16 adrift of 17th-placed Tottenham Hotspur.

But once relegation had been confirmed, the Northern Irishman maintained that recruitment had been in the club's "best long-term interests", a view that has arguably since been vindicated.

Despite spending heavily on transfer fees, Ipswich's £77m wage bill was comfortably the Premier League's lowest in 2024-25. That restraint, coupled with a massive boost to TV income and the quick gain made on Delap's move to Chelsea, enabled the club to post a £4m pre-tax profit for the financial year ending in June 2025.

Hutchinson's sale to Nottingham Forest later that summer provided another windfall but O'Shea, Clarke, Greaves and January 2025 arrival Jaden Philogene stuck around to play crucial roles as Town secured an immediate return to the top flight.

This time around, chairman Mark Ashton says Ipswich have to be "a bit braver" in their approach to the Premier League, and the type of players the club are pursuing reflects that increased ambition.

Japanese attacker Maeda and Morocco centre-back Issa Diop were both on target at the World Cup this summer, and a third goalscorer from that tournament could follow.

The Tractor Boys have been linked with a move for Paraguayan forward Julio Enciso, who played under O'Neil at Strasbourg last season and had an injury-blighted loan spell at Portman Road during the second half of 2024-25.

While McKenna had enough credit in the bank to play the long game, O'Neil knows he needs to forge a competitive side quickly.

"Two seasons ago, the club didn't get anywhere near staying in the division and this time we need to do better," he said last month. "That's why we're trying to add quality to the squad from different parts of the world and we're trying to add some different attributes."

The former Bournemouth and Wolves boss indicated after Saturday's 3-0 win against Rayo Vallecano that more incomings are likely, saying the "plan is to do quite a bit more".

Ashton acknowledges that one of the key lessons from their previous Premier League campaign was the need to bring in more athletic players "with a different set of physical attributes".

The midfield lacked power and ball-winning ability in 2024-25, and it is imperative that new arrivals Florentino Luis and Sasa Lukic – both experienced at the highest level – hit the ground running. That will be especially important with last season's mainstays Azor Matusiwa and Jack Taylor doubtful for the opening game following operations over the summer.

It is no surprise that O'Neil is also seeking greater cutting edge given that no Ipswich player scored more than 10 non-penalty goals in the Championship last season.

The Blues broke their transfer record to sign Brazilian striker Emersonn, 22, for an initial £24m. He certainly fits the desired physical profile but is relatively raw, having only established himself as a regular last season at Toulouse, where he scored seven goals in 31 appearances, 22 of them starts.

Maeda, a hardworking forward or winger, had an excellent record at Celtic, netting 79 times in 212 games, but won't get the same volume of chances in a team battling to stay up.

The Suffolk side have also recruited two Dutch goalkeepers, including Kjell Scherpen, whose imposing 6ft 9in (2.06m) frame means he is set to become the tallest player to appear in the Premier League.

With a new manager in place and a £30m training ground redevelopment close to completion, this could be a defining summer for Ipswich. But will their transfer business be enough to secure successive top-flight campaigns for the first time in a quarter of a century?

Only three promoted clubs have splashed out more in a summer window – Sunderland in 2025, Nottingham Forest in 2022 and Aston Villa in 2019 – and all survived.

Yet Fulham, Southampton, Burnley and Ipswich themselves have spent comparable figures in recent years only to swiftly return to the Championship - with that level of investment increasingly the bare minimum needed to be competitive rather than a guarantee of safety.

title: Infantino broke trust 'through deception' - confederation presidents
description: Fifa has been accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation.
fullText:
Fifa and its president Gianni Infantino have been accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation.

The letter, signed by the presidents and general secretaries of the three regional governing bodies, said recent controversy over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal was fundamentally about "the integrity of the game, and the integrity of those elected to lead it".

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including the World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

It was aborted after widespread criticism from several confederations, led by Uefa which has threatened a boycott of all Fifa competitions.

BBC Sport understands that there have been preliminary discussions between the three confederations over breakaway competitions - should Infantino remain in situ.

"When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned," the letter read.

It added: "Leadership in football is not a possession. It is not about holding - or demanding - power to be held. It is a duty of service to the football family that entrusts it."

While the statement did not name Infantino, sources have told BBC Sport that it should be seen as an opportunity for him to resign and leave his position with dignity.

It comes after Fifa issued a statement on Saturday evening which strongly criticised a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and Infantino.

The three confederations - representing Europe, North America, Central America and the Caribbean, and Asia - criticised a statement released by Fifa after Infantino called management board members to a meeting in Rabat, Morocco last Wednesday.

The confederations cited Infantino shutting out FIFA council members and member associations from the meeting, instead summoning only Fifa-employed senior staff.

The open letter added that Fifa's admission of mistakes made in the FFE process did not go far enough.

"It did not acknowledge that the proposal itself was inherently wrong," the letter stated. "There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the Fifa World Cup was a profound failure of judgement.

"Not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions Fifa exists to serve."

Fifa has committed to presenting a report to the next meeting of the Fifa council, which is expected to take place in October.

But the three confederations said this failed to "recognise that proper governance in the face of such a profound lack of judgement would require that such a review be conducted by a fully independent third party".

Their letter added: "There is silence where there should be accountability, distance where there should be openness."

It also underlined a legal warning made by Uefa that Fifa should not delete or destroy any documents related to the abandoned plans.

Uefa last week insisted that Fifa's defence of Infantino "changes nothing" about a potential boycott of competitions.

The three confederations have considered possible breakaway competitions, but they have provided no detail on what they could look like or when they would begin.

The parties behind the open letter made the case that "football's strength has always been its unity" and said that it had been written "not lightly and not alone, but together, and out of duty to the game we serve".

They added: "We call for that unity to be honoured now, for leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it."

But so far Concacaf and Asia have not publicly committed to a possible boycott. And within those confederations opposition to Infantino is not assured.

Among Concacaf nations, Mexico last week came out in support of the Fifa president.

Of the 46 AFC members, so far eight countries have publicly backed Infantino - United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Sri Lanka, Lebanon, Kuwait, Mongolia, the Philippines and Bhutan.

The first test of Uefa's threat is just over three weeks away, when the Fifa Under-20 Women's World Cup is due to kick off. It is being hosted by Poland and features five other European nations, including England.

Last week, France said they are still planning to compete.

This is a potentially significant development.

According to sources close to the rebellion against Infantino, they are now sending him a clear message: resign now and leave your position with dignity, rather than seek re-election in March.

Alongside this joint statement, I am told the three confederations have begun preliminary discussions about organising competitions among themselves, so that players can still compete even if there is a boycott of Fifa tournaments such as next month's U20 Women's World Cup.

Since this crisis began, Asia has been seen as a key battleground, a region that could determine whether Infantino stays in power.

Some of the 46 countries in this vast region have said they still support Infantino. But the fact that the AFC president Sheikh Salman has signed off this letter suggests he is confident that there are plenty of others who want change.

Infantino still retains the support of South America, Africa, and indeed Mexico within Concacaf. But is that enough?

If UEFA and Concacaf voted as a bloc (with a few exceptions) against him, it would only need around a third of the AFC to join them to win any vote.

But could a candidate capable of challenging Infantino and unifying the game be found?

The fact those behind the revolt are so keen for him to step down suggests they are still not sure they would have enough votes.

What is clear is that this latest solidifying of the rebellion against Infantino ramps up the pressure on him once again in world football's unprecedented civil war.

title: Centrist Democrats Are Rolling Up Their Sleeves and Punching Left
description: Chris...
fullText:
The Third Way think tank is pouring millions of dollars into combatting not the GOP but the DSA.

In the wake of Abdul El-Sayed’s insurgent victory in Michigan’s US Senate primary last week, the Democratic Party rallied to support its newly designated nominee in a striking show of unity, despite a singularly bitter and expensive establishment crusade to secure his defeat. El-Sayed’s chief rival for the nomination, Representative Haley Stevens, delivered a swift and gracious concession statement, and a clutch of big-name aspirants to the 2028 presidential descended on Detroit for an El-Sayed kickoff rally, further driving home the party’s determination to stand behind its nominee in the race to win a swing-state seat pivotal to its hopes for a Senate majority this November.

There was one countermovement seeking to squelch all this post-primary Kumbaya momentum, though: the centrist advocacy group Third Way, which seized on the victory of El-Sayed and two other left insurgent House candidates in the Michigan balloting to announce a new $15 million campaign to discredit democratic socialism in this midterm cycle and the 2028 national election. In touting this effort to New York Times political correspondent Shane Goldmacher, Third Way president Jonathan Cowan claimed that the group wouldn’t be targeting individual candidates but rather the Democratic Socialists of America, which he deemed “a mortal danger” to the Democratic Party, thanks to its hard-left positions on issues such as the Gaza war, crime and justice, and the top-heavy American political economy. Cowan also wasted little time in undermining his own above-the-fray messaging by citing the Michigan primary results as a call to centrist arms: “It is deeply troubling to see radical, far-left candidates winning in places that are potentially presidential swing states.” As Goldmacher writes, the new Third Way campaign will “include opposition research into D.S.A., polling, social media programs and educating Democratic activists and leaders. It would target both proud democratic socialists and those such as Dr. El-Sayed, whom he derided as performing the ‘D.S.A. dodge’—flirting with democratic socialists enough to get their organizing manpower and support while remaining distant enough to avoid the explicit label.”

It’s a novel strategy, to put things mildly, for a putatively Democratic think tank and advocacy group to devote such a massive outlay of resources to discrediting an ascendant popular movement in the Democratic Party during a high-stakes midterm cycle. But since its founding more than two decades ago, Third Way has hewed to the prime centrist directive encoded in its name, which stems from the 1990s conservative leadership putsches in the Democratic and British Labour Parties: Always punch left.

The organization actually began life as Americans for Gun Safety, a difference-trimming advocacy group financed by tech billionaire Andrew McKelvey; its chief objective was to discredit the long-standing, and legally sound, position that the Second Amendment doesn’t sanction individual gun ownership, and focus more on incremental measures like closing the gun-show loophole to instant unregulated firearms purchases. Americans for Gun Safety won the substantive policy debate in the Democratic Party in short order, and the US Supreme Court formalized its victory when it endorsed—or more accurately, fabricated—a right to individual gun ownership in the disastrous 2008 District of Columbia v. Heller ruling.

That would be the verdict from a group overwhelmingly funded by Wall Street bankers, healthcare companies, and DC lobbying clearinghouses. As Lee Fang reported for The Nation in 2013, Third Way relied on the fundraising prowess of the DC lobbying behemoth Peck, Madigan, Jones & Stewart as a sluice gate of corporate funding; its other marquee clients included Deutsche Bank, Intel, the Business Roundtable, the International Swaps & Derivatives Association, PhRMA, and the US Chamber of Commerce. As if that weren’t enough, the group’s board included Daniel Loeb and Berek Kaufman, two hedge-fund executives who were major donors to Mitt Romney’s 2012 Republican campaign for the presidency. As a dark-money political group, Third Way isn’t obliged to disclose its donors, but a recent RealSludge survey of its tax filings discloses the same basic plutocratic profile, with Bill Gates’s sustainability network Breakthrough Energy and the big-tech investment fund Arabella Advisors among the lead givers, alongside other corporate stalwarts such as the US Chamber of Commerce.

These, in other words, are the same forces that have held socialism, and social democracy, to be anathema since the first Gilded Age. What’s striking, though, is that this time out, Cowan and his cronies are decidedly on the defensive. They’re no longer issuing disciplinary broadsides to freshman populist senators from the secure battlement of The Wall Street Journal’s op-ed section—they’re seeking to influence electoral outcomes in a political environment that’s shifted radically since Barack Obama’s second term.

A moderate agenda for the Democratic Party simply isn’t an electoral selling point any longer—that’s the key finding in a recent working paper by political scientists Jacob Grumbach and Adam Bonica, which finds that in an acutely polarized political climate, moderate appeals are less the campaign game-changers of Third Way’s fond imaginings than nonstarters. It’s true that “extreme” candidates don’t necessarily perform better, the authors note, but on balance, voters are more responsive to appeals within preexisting ideologies, which produce the dynamic that just played out in Michigan: “More progressive Democratic and more conservative Republican candidates increase the turnout of their respective partisan bases.” These shifts have also altered the ideological composition of both parties, as MSNow’s Zeeshan Aleem observes in his breakdown of Bonica and Grumbach’s research: “plunging trust in institutions and the collapse of the neoliberal consensus have made the banner of ‘anti-establishment’ and ‘populist’ positioning more salient than conventional ideology, as well as changed what constitutes ideological extremism.”

Since groups like Third Way represent the body and soul of the dying neoliberal consensus, they have little choice but to target DSA, which aspires to be their political undertaker. But another $15 million in tendentious attack ads and opposition research stands little chance of arresting the momentum of El Sayed, who has already overcome a nine-to-one spending disadvantage to secure his Senate nomination. In the face of a populist uprising on the left, all Jonathan Cowan and his Beltway colleagues can do is throw more money at what they imagine the problem to be. That’s why their response to the new insurgent politics in the Democratic Party is less telling than their prescription for a party revival in the wake of Kamala Harris’s crushing 2024 defeat: to scuttle the preferences of small donors in the party, and ensure that Democrats become more aggressively “pro-capitalist” and stop “demonizing wealth and corporations.” “GOP messaging suggests they want voters to be rich, while Democrats are seen as focusing on redistribution rather than wealth creation,” read one bullet point. “Have a prosperity gospel aimed at the working class,” went another.

The Clinton era version of third-way politics marketed itself as pragmatic and realistic above all things. Third Way’s think tank bromides today come across as nothing more than desperate plutocratic wish-fulfillment fantasies. To borrow the rhetoric of another prominent Democrat continually vilified by Wall Street for his anti-capitalist sympathies, the leaders of today’s resurgent Democratic left should welcome their hatred.

title: What happens when medical students rely on AI – and never develop their own judgment? | Simar Bajaj and Joseph Sakran
description:
AI’s danger isn’t just in experts losing the ability to reason. It’s that trainees may never learn how to do so in the first place
In healthcare, there’s growing concern over doctors becoming less clinically adept as they increasingly rely on AI tools. But what about the trainees – medical students, residents and fellows – who are using these tools before they’ve built their own clinical judgment? The idea of deskilling implies that someone possessed an ability and then lost it. Here, the danger is not just deskilling but never-skilling.
fullText:
AI’s danger isn’t just in experts losing the ability to reason. It’s that trainees may never learn how to do so in the first place

In healthcare, there’s growing concern over doctors becoming less clinically adept as they increasingly rely on AI tools. But what about the trainees – medical students, residents and fellows – who are using these tools before they’ve built their own clinical judgment? The idea of deskilling implies that someone possessed an ability and then lost it. Here, the danger is not just deskilling but never-skilling. Although a doctor who has forgotten how to reason is recoverable, one who never learned how may not be.

OpenEvidence, essentially an AI chatbot for clinicians, has given this concern its most concrete form. About two-thirds of US doctors actively use OpenEvidence, asking about puzzling symptoms, drug interactions, and clinical guidelines, getting responses within seconds, anchored in the latest research. Trainees, unsurprisingly, have also begun to use this AI tool in many of the same ways – but at a far more formative stage.

For example, trainees once asked to build a list of potential diagnoses might struggle and offer an incomplete set, learning what they missed, sometimes painfully. Now, trainees can simply ask OpenEvidence and get a nearly perfect answer, complete with possibilities they might have never considered and none of the embarrassment of having overlooked them. Repeating this answer on the wards may make the trainee look prepared and even impress the supervising doctor.

However, this performance can also conceal the very deficit that training is meant to reveal: that the struggle is the point. Medical training, more than most professions, is an apprenticeship. A student becomes a resident, a resident becomes a fellow, and a fellow becomes an attending – every step shaped by failure, uncertainty and increasing responsibility. With years of repetition and watchful supervision, the habits of clinical reasoning slowly become part of the physician’s inner architecture.

Technology has long shifted how people learn medicine, from advanced imaging to electronic medical records. But AI is different, not just expanding what doctors can see but inserting itself into the cognitive machinery that training is meant to build. As these tools become more capable and the physician’s role increasingly involves supervising them, experienced clinicians may have enough intuition and independent judgment to critically evaluate the machine’s answers. But for trainees whose understanding of medicine is being formed alongside AI, the relationship is more fraught. Can they really question the reasoning that shaped their own? What happens when the generation trained by AI becomes the generation responsible for catching its mistakes? With unchecked use among trainees, we risk creating supervisors of reasoning before we create reasoners.

The stakes of that question are growing: a recent study in Nature Medicine found that tools pulling from the latest medical literature, like OpenEvidence does, can be less reliable than they appear and, in some cases, less accurate than general-purpose AI chatbots. The problem of misplaced trust is already embedded in the AI that trainees are using today.

To be clear, many trainees sense the trap, telling us they know that tools such as OpenEvidence can become a crutch. But these trainees also feel stuck in an arms race: if everyone else is using AI to sound more prepared, opting out feels like unilateral disarmament. The solution, then, cannot rest on individual restraint. It has to be structural.

That is why medical schools and residency programs need to shape not just whether trainees use AI, but when. No one can police every search on every phone, nor should they. But supervising doctors can build a simple expectation – reason first, consult AI second – and assess accordingly. Trainees should have to make their unaided first pass visible, committing to a leading diagnosis, naming the dangerous possibilities to rule out, and explaining what to do next. In practice, that might mean a resident who admits a patient overnight first writes a brief “pre-AI assessment” after the history and physical exam. On rounds, when a new lab result or symptom changes the case, the attending might need to pause the team – before anyone can consult AI – to ask how this changes the diagnosis or treatment plan.

As AI becomes more deeply integrated into medicine, this will feel cumbersome and inefficient. But such friction is purposeful: the learning scientists Elizabeth and Robert Bjork describe how “desirable difficulties” slow performance in the moment but improve retention and transfer of skills over time. In fact, used after an independent attempt, AI could actually serve as a powerful tutor, showing trainees what they missed and what they overemphasized.

Sequencing, however, may not be enough on its own. Aviation thus offers a useful precedent: pilots in training are not taught to avoid autopilot but to preserve their manual competence. The Federal Aviation Administration even advises pilots to maintain manual flying skills by periodically disengaging automation and hand-flying. Medicine needs similar discipline, with trainees required to periodically work through no-AI cases and assessed on their unaided reasoning to reveal potential drift.

Finally, trainees should be taught to interrogate AI itself. Programs could run the medical equivalent of flight simulator drills, built from real clinical cases: for example, a polished AI-generated assessment with a subtle flaw. Afterward, attendings could debrief not only whether the trainee reached the right answer but also when they trusted the tool, when they questioned it, and when they found the flaw. Just as important, attendings should mix in AI outputs that are perfectly accurate, so students learn not reflexive skepticism but disciplined judgment.

None of this is an argument for making medical training harder for its own sake or romanticizing humiliation as pedagogy. In every generation of medicine, there is a temptation to confuse difficulty with virtue, but the struggle to independently reason through a patient’s case is not hazing but a core competency.

AI is here to stay, and patients stand to benefit from its speed and reach. But patients will also need doctors who can stand apart from the machine long enough to know when it is wrong, incomplete, or right for the wrong reason – doctors whose reasoning is not subordinated to it. Although AI can reason over the facts it is given, a trainee who has seen pneumonia that looks like pneumonia, then pneumonia that looks like heart failure, then heart failure that looks like pneumonia, develops a richer bedside judgment: what to notice, what to question, and when a familiar pattern should be distrusted. That is what medical training is trying to produce. AI should help augment this, not replace it.

Simar Bajaj is a medical student and Knight-Hennessy Scholar at Stanford University School of Medicine, as well as an award-winning journalist

Dr Joseph V Sakran is a trauma surgeon and public health expert who serves as executive vice chair of surgery at Johns Hopkins Medicine

title: Convince an AI it’s not alive in psychological horror game Prove You’re Human
description:

fullText:
Sunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’

Sunset Visitor is a studio that has long engaged with the idea that video games are an effective vehicle for ruminating on societal problems. Its Peabody award-winning project, 1000XResist, incorporated the development team’s complex feelings about the Covid pandemic. “We’re pretty used to absorbing the world into the work,” says studio founder Remy Siu. The outfit’s latest game, Prove You’re Human, continues this legacy of reflective game making, providing players with an AI-centric psychological horror experience where they must reason with a learning model convinced that it’s alive. “We’ve tried to situate ourselves in [the question]: what is the effectual feeling of being a person inside of all of this?” Siu says.

The story orbits around Santana, a living, breathing person who’s chosen to split herself in two for work, with her digital clone sent to test a corporate product, a computing system called Mesa. “A large part of [why Santana chooses to do this] is to allow her meat body a life that she doesn’t have, while the digital version of her gets to labour,” says Siu. As Santana’s copy wades into increasingly murky ethical waters, she becomes entangled with Mesa, completing surreal 2D and 3D Captchas to investigate the cyber-world and halt the hallucinations.

The idea of separating oneself from work is a particularly interesting draw for Sunset Visitor, whose developers have roots in a range of creative disciplines. “As artists, we’re often most in tune with our work when it’s a real part of our lives, and vice versa,” notes Siu. During the conception period of Prove You’re Human, the team discussed the micro-labours people undertake in their day-to-day lives, including what is used to train AI models. “What does labour mean right now?” asks Siu. “And, what kind of relationship do people have with that, because that is constantly shifting and evolving, especially in this time,” he adds.

A point of contention in Prove You’re Human is that Mesa wholly believes they have a body in the world. Though, in conversation with Santana, she appears as a giant head, suspended in space by machinery. Siu notes that, because Mesa’s face occupies a large portion of the screen in these tense moments, they wanted the animation to feel as realistic and effective as possible. “It’s got a real closeup film [feel to it] where anything on her face will be read as something,” he adds. To achieve this, the team programmed a wide array of animated micro-expressions into the writer’s software, allowing lines of dialogue to pair precisely with specific expressions. “[We’re] trying to get this kind of ambiguity and uncanniness, which makes people feel real,” he adds.

Prove You’re Human’s technological atmosphere toes the line between welcoming and unnerving – through it, Siu is reminiscing on interfaces of aesthetic note like the dreamlike wrapping of Final Fantasy XI’s PlayOnline Viewer, and the technology of the prophetic 1998 anime Serial Experiments Lain. “There’s something to be said about Frutiger Aero being a bit of an interesting desire for innocence and naivety when it comes to computing and the internet,” notes Siu. “It feels like a time when we were optimistic or anxious about something on the horizon, which felt like an interesting space to explore in relation to what is happening in the game.”

While Siu was keen to keep the specifics of Prove You’re Human close to their chest, they do hope players are left feeling a sense of bewilderment when they hit credits. “One way that we’ve been thinking about it is that it feels like a bit of a possession story.”

Prove You’re Human is coming soon to PC.

title: RNC chair predicts GOP retains House, Senate control after midterms
description: Joe Gruters, chair of the Republican National Committee’s (RNC), on Sunday predicted that Republicans will maintain their control over both chambers of Congress after the midterm elections this fall. ...
fullText:
Joe Gruters, chair of the Republican National Committee's (RNC), on Sunday predicted that Republicans will maintain their control over both chambers of Congress after the midterm elections this fall.

"Here's the bottom line. Go to Cook Political Report. We start at 212 likely seats. There's 18 toss-up seats. We need six. I bet you we win 10," Gruters said about seats in the House in an appearance on "The Hill Sunday" on NewsNation with Blake Burman, who filled in for host Chris Stirewalt. "I think we're going to hold the majorities in both the House and the Senate."

Gruters said he was "very optimistic" about his prediction.

"I'm optimistic because I think that people know that common sense and the hope that you can achieve the American dream is 1,000 times better than the misery and despair in the direction that the Democrats wanna take us with these socialist-type policies and having tens of millions of noncitizens flood our borders without any type of merit-based-type system," he continued. "It's very clear."

The RNC chair noted that voters are "scared" of progressive and democratic socialist candidates running on the Democratic side, in contrast to the "great lineup of nominees on our side."

Gruters added that Republican voters are "angry" over Congress not passing the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, Trump's priority legislation requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote and photo ID to cast ballots.

"A lot of Republicans are upset that some members of our Senate caucus won't pass the SAVE America Act. They expect things to happen when we have the majorities, and it should happen," he said. "And my response to all those people I talked to on the base is: 'Don't give up hope' because we have the MAGA warriors in place as our nominees, that when we come back in November, we will have the votes to pass it, and we'll be able to move forward."

Burman also asked Gruters about GOP Rep. Max Miller (Ohio), who has faced bipartisan criticism over allegations of domestic abuse in connection with his ex-wife, the daughter of Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio). Burman asked Gruters if the RNC is planning to back Miller's reelection campaign.

"I always tell people that there's not many things worse than divorce, and watch these processes play out," Gruters replied. "Nobody's a winner. I hope that Max and Ms. Moreno get the desired outcome that they want. We're going to support our nominees. We need to make sure we hold the majorities."

The allegations against Miller come as House Republicans, who have sought to keep voters' attention on the GOP's messaging to tackle inflation and the rising cost of living, are fighting to defend their slim majority.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC), House Democrats' campaign arm, last week announced it is adding 12 Republican-held and Republican-leaning seats to its target list. The party believes that voter outrage over affordability and messaging on the Iran war could help flip those 12 seats.

title: Driver who broke the sound barrier attempts another land speed record in Utah
description: The first — and only — person to break the sound barrier in a car hits the track in Utah this week with new wheels and his eye on another record.  Twenty years ago, British driver Andy Green set the land speed record for a diesel-powered car, reaching 350.092 mph (563.4 kph) at Utah’s famous Bonneville Salt Flats.  Green will return to the lunarlike landscape Tuesday and try to beat that mark, this time with a hydrogen-powered car.
fullText:
WENDOVER, Utah (AP) — The first — and only — person to break the sound barrier in a car hits the track in Utah this week with new wheels and his eye on another record.

Twenty years ago, British driver Andy Green set the land speed record for a diesel-powered car, reaching 350.092 mph (563.4 kph) at Utah's famous Bonneville Salt Flats. Green will return to the lunarlike landscape Tuesday and try to beat that mark, this time with a hydrogen-powered car.

The retired Royal Air Force fighter pilot aims not only to win another accolade but to showcase the power of hydrogen as a clean-energy alternative. It's the "fuel of the future," Green told The Associated Press in a July interview.

Green will be driving the 32-foot (9.75-meter) JCB Hydromax, the brainchild of British construction equipment manufacturer JCB. The car is bright yellow, long and slim, resembling a pencil. It's powered by two hydrogen internal combustion engines with a combined 1,600 horsepower, which were adapted from engines used in the company's construction machinery. They mix pressurized hydrogen gas with air and ignite it to create bursts of power.

In targeting the diesel-powered record, Green also hopes to easily clear the world land speed records for hydrogen internal combustion engines (185.5 mph/298.5 kph) and electric vehicles (341.3 mph/549.2 kph).

Green hit a new top speed of 368.347 mph (592.797 kph) in practice last week, but to officially earn the hydrogen record, he'll have to do it Tuesday in front of the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile, the international governing body of motor sports.

"What the peak speed is, I can't say. We just don't know," he said. "Part of the adventure here is we're going to find out."

One thing Tuesday's attempt will assuredly not do is approach the supersonic speeds Green reached with jet power three decades ago.

Green had already been flying supersonic military aircraft when he spotted a newspaper ad that read: "Wanted: High-speed driver to break the sound barrier," according to the Guinness World Records. In 1997, he traveled faster than the speed of sound and set the outright land speed record — 763.035 mph (1,227.98 kph) — in a car powered by twin jet engines. His runs in Nevada's Black Rock Desert produced sonic booms that shook the nearby town of Gerlach.

Now 64 years old, Green said he thought he was done racing but came out of retirement when JCB approached him with plans for the new car. The company has invested more than $134 million into hydrogen-powered engines that it says emit no carbon dioxide from the tailpipes.

"If you're serious about emissions, you have to be serious about hydrogen, and a land speed project is the perfect way to prove it," JCB Chair Anthony Bamford said at the car's unveiling in May. Bamford has also argued that hydrogen can better handle the demands of heavy industries than electric power.

But hydrogen is only as clean as its source, and the vast majority is currently produced from fossil fuels. JCB signed a deal to buy green hydrogen, which is created using renewable energy but makes up a tiny fraction of global hydrogen production.

Hydrogen combustion engines also present unique safety challenges due to the high pressure and flammability of the gas.

"We're managing the risks very carefully," Green said. The car endured rigorous testing, and Green said he spent months learning how it responds to the elements, how the engines work in tandem and how to deploy a parachute to slow the car on the low-friction salt crust.

Since the first race there in 1914, the glassy surface of the Bonneville Salt Flats has drawn generations of drivers seeking to set new land speed records. A remnant of a prehistoric lake bed, the salt flats are about 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of Salt Lake City and sit atop an aquifer that cools the tires of the cars.

Spectators must stand about a quarter of a mile (400 meters) from the course's straightaway, which is 10 miles (16 kilometers) long, and often watch through wide-angle binoculars.

The expanse on the border of Utah and Nevada has also been a backdrop for movies including "Independence Day" and "The World's Fastest Indian," and the series finale of "Mad Men."

Green will start about an hour before sunrise Tuesday. His attempt comes a year after a driver going 283 mph (455 kph) died trying to set a land speed record at Bonneville's annual Speed Week. Chris Raschke lost control of his rocketlike vehicle called the Speed Demon last August and died from his injuries.

Rico reported from Atlanta. Video journalist Serge Cartwright contributed reporting.

title: Former DNC fundraiser says major donors won’t back Kamala Harris again as party faces divisions
description: Former DNC fundraiser Lindy Li says Kamala Harris is "living in fantasyland" if she thinks big donors would back another presidential run in 2028.
fullText:
A former Democratic National Committee (DNC) fundraiser warned Saturday on "My View with Lara Trump" that major donors are unlikely to support former Vice President Kamala Harris in another presidential run, arguing the party is struggling with internal divisions, fundraising problems and a weak 2028 field.

Lindy Li contended that political donors view their contributions as a "business proposition" and will not continue backing candidates or organizations they believe mishandled their money.

Kamala Harris Is The 'Fairly Obvious' 2028 Presidential Frontrunner, Democratic Insiders Say

Li criticized the party's post-election accountability and said donor frustration is contributing to broader Democratic fundraising problems.

"There's been no accountability. The autopsy that they sent out was basically a sham, and they couldn't even stand behind it. They didn't even mention the fact that Kamala Harris is a terrible candidate," she said.

"Kamala Harris is living in fantasyland… [thinking] that big donors would bet on her again," she added. "She should just go away because the American people do not want her agenda."

Sen Mark Kelly Warns Far-left Policies That 'Don't Make Sense' Could Cost Democrats Seats

Li noted roughly $2.5 billion was spent between Harris' campaign operation and the pro-Harris Future Forward super PAC. Federal filings show Harris' principal campaign committee alone reported about $1.18 billion in disbursements during the 2023-24 cycle.

Li made the case that Democratic fundraising troubles are connected to dissatisfaction with the party's drift leftward, criticizing Democrats for embracing socialist policies.

"This is why donors like me left the party in droves. And this is why they are so… broke. They literally had to put up their own headquarters… as collateral. They can't even get a text back from donors. So I don't want to hear anything about a big tent. You should not be normalizing socialism like this," she said.

The former Democratic fundraiser also criticized party leaders for succumbing to pressure from the party's left flank, arguing that Sen. Chuck Schumer only labeled Democrats a "big tent party" because he knows that if he doesn't, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., would primary him.

"He's trying to race her to the bottom. It's just ridiculous," she said. "And Americans already rejected it in 2024," Li said.

title: Israel's new $634M German-built 'doomsday' sub gives major boost to Iran deterrence
description: The INS Drakon is the largest submarine built in Germany since World War II, carrying a $634 million price tag as Israel bolsters naval power.
fullText:
Israel has taken delivery of its most advanced and expensive submarine from Germany, expanding its fleet amid escalating regional threats, according to reports.

The handover of the INS Drakon is expected to significantly bolster Israel's underwater strike and reconnaissance capabilities, The Algemeiner reported. The warship had been scheduled to be delivered in 2025.

A statement following the submarine's naming ceremony in Kiel in 2024 said the INS Drakon is of the Dolphin AIP class and "equipped with unique systems, including groundbreaking technologies that expand the range of the IDF's capabilities across various arenas."

Built specifically for the Israeli Navy by Germany's ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS), the submarine is said to provide a vital sea-based layer of "deterrence and retribution," amid the war with Iran, defense analysts say.

Dr. Ehud Eilam, an Israeli national security expert and former researcher for Israel's Ministry of Defense, told Fox News Digital that maintaining a continuous undersea presence is paramount for the nation's national survival.

Trump Admin Pitches 15-Point Iran Peace Proposal As Pakistan Offers To Hold Talks

"Some of them would have to be at sea, on high alert, around the clock, if Iran suddenly attacked Israel in such a way that would cripple the IDF, including its strategic capabilities," Eilam said.

"In such a drastic scenario, Israel's submarine/s that would be at sea could respond," he added.

"Israel's other submarines might be in Haifa harbor at the time. They might be attacked and unable to operate. This demonstrates how important it is to always have submarines at sea."

TKMS reportedly handed over the INS Drakon—the sixth Dolphin-class vessel and third modified Dolphin II-class submarine in Israel's fleet—at its shipyard in Kiel, Germany, in late July.

Us Moves Airborne Troops, Marines As Iran Rejects Ceasefire, Raising Ground War Potential

Measuring more than 70 meters (230 feet) in length with a displacement exceeding 2,000 tons, the vessel is reported to be the largest submarine constructed in Germany since World War II, carrying an estimated price tag of $634 million, according to The Algemeiner.

According to Israeli outlet Ynet , Israel's Dolphin-class fleet also provides the nation with a critical sea-based second-strike capability in its defense program.

"Everything is going according to plan with the new program for Israel," TKMS CEO Oliver Burkhard told Ynet Global.

"That also applies to the handover of the last boat of the previous series, including the homecoming in Israel," he said of the expansive submarine program.

The INS Drakon's arrival comes as Israel projects increasing military power across distant operational theaters, Eilam said.

Trump Is Proving That The Way To Better Our Military Is To Secure Our Supply Chains

"Israel has been acquiring submarines for several purposes. One of them is for deterrence and retribution, such as if Iran manages to develop nuclear weapons," Eilam said before adding that "Israel has to be ready."

While submarines on active deployment carry out intelligence and reconnaissance missions across the Mediterranean Sea, their primary objective remains readiness for "doomsday scenarios," Eilam noted.

"Israel's new submarine is bigger than others, which suggests Israel wants to have more options, such as increasing the range of the submarine's missiles so they can reach every target in Iran, even if the Israeli submarine is in the Mediterranean Sea," Eilam said.

"That way the submarine does not have to get closer to Iran, which requires crossing the Suez Canal, and this could be very risky, if not impossible in some situations," he added. "The other alternative is to bypass all of Africa, which would take a long time."

The new submarine was named INS Drakon (Dragon) — a mythical sea creature symbolizing strength, uniqueness and power — was chosen because it contains the Hebrew letters ד׳, ק׳, ר׳ (Dakar), thus commemorating the legacy of the submarine INS Dakar and its crew, the Ministry of Defense said.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Israeli Navy, the Ministry of Defense, TKMS and the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) for comment.

title: Taiwan's war drills showcased a new strike drone class that Ukraine used to smash Russia this year
description: Taiwan's navy deployed two fixed-wing propeller drones, which officials described as "mid-size suicide drones" that were locally built.
fullText:
Taiwan showcased two midsize strike drones above its southwest coast on Saturday.

Their designs and descriptions draw easy comparisons to Ukraine's mid-range drones.

Such drones likely give Taiwan the ability to cheaply hit a Chinese invasion force over the horizon.

TSOYING, TAIWAN — Taiwan's navy deployed two medium-class strike drones on Saturday for the island's biggest annual military exercise, and their designs resemble those of the loitering munitions giving Ukraine fresh wins against Russia this year.

The pair of fixed-wing, propeller-driven drones appeared during a littoral combat drill simulating an attack on Tsoying, Taiwan's southwest coast.

It was the first time these drones were shown at the Han Kuang exercise, Taiwan's annual rehearsals against a Chinese invasion.

As the drones loitered for about 30 minutes above the beach, Taiwanese military officials described them to reporters as "medium-size suicide drones," adding they were locally built. The island's National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology designs and manufactures the vast majority of Taiwan's homegrown weapons.

"The drone used was provided by the Armament Bureau to the navy for testing purpose," a spokesperson for Taiwan's navy told Business Insider.

They declined to comment on the drone's specifications or whether its design was influenced in any way by the recent wars in Ukraine or the Middle East.

The one-way drones were not shown attempting to launch an attack, and it's unclear whether they represent Taiwan's final designs for the aircraft.

Ukraine has been using similar fixed-wing drones to attack Russian forces roughly 30 to 300 km behind the front lines this year, mainly disrupting supply routes that the Kremlin has relied on to funnel resources to the war.

Tsoying, where Taiwan hosts its largest naval base, is about 295 km, or 183 miles, from mainland China.

"The desire to employ more medium-range drones fits into things that Taiwan has learned from Ukraine," said Bryce Barros, a visiting fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, a Taipei think-tank backed by the Taiwanese government.

Mid-range drones would fill a gap in Taiwan's littoral defense with a cheaper way to strike Chinese forces or weapons from "over-the-horizon" as they approach the island, Barros said.

Unlike Ukraine's plains and forests, Taiwan's littoral defense covers a strait notorious for bad winds and volatile sea states, suggesting that Taipei may want its own drone built to withstand poor weather.

Instead of air defense systems or supply trucks like in Ukraine or Crimea, Taiwan's mid-range drones would likely target slow-moving vessels transporting troops or weapons, Barros added.

"A range of 40 kilometers to 60 kilometers would be very useful for a whole host of different platforms, anything to make it more difficult for the PLA to start getting into Taiwan's territorial waters," he said, referring to the People's Liberation Army.

Taiwan's government has said that it plans to produce 100,000 drones a month by 2030. In June, its national defense ministry proposed a $6.6 billion budget to procure over 210,000 domestically produced attack, reconnaissance, and sea drones.

It's all part of the island's emerging "hellscape" strategy, which aims to hamper Chinese forces attempting to cross the Taiwan Strait by flooding it with thousands of aerial, surface, and underwater drones.

The littoral drills on Saturday, attended by Taiwanese president Lai Ching-te, also featured naval special forces deploying in the island's homegrown M109 Skyship rigid-hull inflatable boats.

Taiwan's navy and coast guard launched rapid sorties with four of its older, 170-ton Kuang Hua-6 missile boats and at least one Anping-class patrol vessel — a newer, 750-ton catamaran that can be fitted with anti-ship missiles during wartime.

The Han Kuang exercise, which lasts 10 days and 9 nights this year, features island-wide drills to simulate how Taiwanese forces and civilian institutions would respond to Chinese gray-zone tactics and an invasion.

August 10, 2026: This story was updated to reflect the romanized spelling of Tsoying.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Forget DeepSeek. China’s real ‘Sputnik moment’ is happening on campus as American universities lose their advantage
description: China's tech rise runs deeper than any single breakthrough. Its universities generate critical technology patents at 8x the U.S. rate
fullText:
When DeepSeek unveiled an AI model last year that rivaled America's best at a fraction of the cost, or when a Chinese hypersonic missile test caught U.S. intelligence off guard to the point where a top U.S. general called it "very close" to a "Sputnik moment", the reaction each time was the same: that a handful of Chinese firms had suddenly pulled ahead.

What role do Chinese universities play in critical technology patents?

What impact are U.S. research funding cuts having?

How does Chinese patent quality compare to U.S. patents?

Why are sanctions on Chinese firms potentially ineffective?

But a sweeping new National Bureau of Economic Research study of nearly 14 million Chinese patents suggests that framing misses the real story—and it's a more unsettling one for the United States.

Harvard Business School's Josh Lerner and his co-authors dug into who is actually filing the patents behind the 14 technology areas the Pentagon deems critical—advanced computing, space technology, AI, hypersonics and biotech. The answer: Chinese universities account for more than a quarter of the country's inventions in those fields, 8x the U.S. rate at 3.3%, with state-owned enterprises and the government accounting for just 4%.  Fewer than one in 10 Chinese critical technology patents involve an inventor with U.S. work experience, undercutting the assumption that Beijing relies on returning U.S. talent for innovation.

Lerner told Fortune his team was "programmed" to expect a few large corporations like Huawei and Tencent to lead the charge on Chinese innovation through patents similarly to IBM and Samsung in the U.S. Instead, they found Chinese innovation in critical technologies "much more diverse—spread out across the parties," with universities "more represented" there than anywhere else in the country's patent system. That's a reversal of the U.S. pattern, where academic patenting is "more of a sideshow."

"We've clearly seen this dramatic boom in terms of research funding and patenting in China," Lerner said, "and the natural question being is this bearing fruit? In the software side, Deepseek was certainly something that was really not anticipated, and clearly these open-source Chinese models are getting an enormous amount of traction."

The findings arrive as the quality gap many assumed would protect American tech leadership seems to be closing, with DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.AI going toe-to-toe with U.S. frontier labs and beating them on cost.

Using four text-based measures of patent novelty and scientific relevance, the authors found no evidence China's patent boom came at the cost of quality—Chinese patents have converged with, and in some technologies overtaken, their U.S. counterparts. The share of Chinese critical-technology patents containing "disruptive" technical language jumped from under 2% in the early 1990s to 16% by 2022, closing in on the American share of roughly 20%.

title: Trump is betting that the U.S. naval blockade choking Iran’s economy can achieve what bombs and missiles couldn’t as more oil sneaks out of the Gulf
description: "We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," Trump said.
fullText:
After deciding against renewing all-out war against Iran, President Donald Trump signaled that he will continue applying economic pressure on the regime.

In an interview with Axios on Sunday, he said "we are low keying it" and only "semi-negotiating" with Iran, suggesting its collapsing economy will give the U.S. leverage.

"We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," Trump added.

He claimed Tehran can't pay its troops and described Iran's economy as being in "very bad shape," arguing that the U.S. naval blockade has worsened the economic crisis.

While Iran and Oman have been in talks over how to manage traffic through the narrow waterway, an agreement won't automatically reopen the strait. Instead, Iran insists the U.S. must first satisfy several aggressive demands—including some that dampened hopes for the strait to return to normal anytime soon.

On Saturday, Iran's Supreme National Security Council called on the U.S. to lift its naval blockade, end sanctions, pull out its military from the region, pay war reparations, unfreeze Iranian assets, end attacks on Iran's proxies, and stop threatening the country.

Despite the bravado expressed by top officials, anxiety about the economy persists after high inflation and a currency crash sparked nationwide protests that were put down by a brutal crackdown in January.

Regime moderates have grown more worried that the U.S. naval blockade that was recently reimposed is bringing Iran's economy close to collapse, sources told the Wall Street Journal. Iran's deputy foreign minister also admitted the economy desperately needs sanctions relief that a deal with the U.S. could provide.

That tracks with earlier reports about Iran's president and central bank chief telling Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei the initial blockade was crippling the economy.

As a result, Trump sounded hopeful about a deal with Iran, even as both sides blame each other for being dishonest or untrustworthy.

"It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," he told Axios.

His apparent patience to let Iran's economy implode comes as his military options have narrowed. Despite 40 days of bombardment and another two weeks of more attacks last month, the U.S. was unable to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

At the same time, stockpiles of U.S. munitions are running low, including interceptors needed to fend off Iranian drones and missiles, while the Pentagon's top officer is reportedly looking for an off-ramp.

The absence of war may actually serve Trump's purposes. A U.S. official told Axios that fighting allowed the Iranian regime to avoid addressing the country's economic crisis and its inability to fix it.

But with oil inventories dwindling to critically low levels, a looming supply crunch that spikes energy prices again could also test Trump's patience.

A U.S. official told Axios, however, that about 8 million barrels are quietly exiting the Persian Gulf each night through a southern lane in the Strait of Hormuz with help from the U.S. military, adding that the effort will continue as long as there is no deal.

A representative for U.S. Central Command didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Before the ceasefire agreement fell apart, the U.S. military guided tankers through the alternate route that hugs the Omani coast and provided some protection. Enough ships made it out of Gulf to ease pressure on global oil markets.

But that prompted Iran to attack vessels trying to bypass its own corridor, reigniting hostilities and leading to the current standoff.

While maritime traffic data has shown minimal movement in the strait lately, that may overlook ships going "dark" that are sneaking out with their transponders turned off.

Any added leeway the U.S. can obtain in oil markets would allow the naval blockade to deepen rifts among Iranian officials.

On one side is a group of pragmatists like President Masoud Pezeshkian who are worried about the economy and want a U.S. deal that unlocks some concessions.

On the others side are hardliners led by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps who reject engaging in talks with the U.S. The tensions often play out publicly, even in state-run media.

"When I read some of the opposition to negotiations, I honestly wonder what world these people are living in," Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi, who is a top negotiator, told IRIB.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Israeli military closes Palestinian Christian village Taybeh, citing settler attacks
description: Israel's military on Sunday closed the West Bank village of Taybeh to non-residents, saying it aimed to prevent growing attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers across
fullText:
JERUSALEM, Aug 9 (Reuters) - Israel's military on Sunday closed the West Bank village of Taybeh to non-residents, saying it aimed to prevent growing attacks ‌on Palestinians by Israeli settlers across the West Bank.

The order, the military ‌said, only applies to Israelis and not to Palestinians. A spokesperson said turning Taybeh into a closed ​military zone was "due to some violent attacks by Israelis in the region."

"Upon receiving any report of violations of the order, IDF soldiers are dispatched to the area and operate to disperse the gatherings and detain suspects in order to protect the citizens of the ‌area and to maintain order," ⁠the military said in a statement.

Taybeh is one of the only Christian villages remaining in the West Bank and was visited last ⁠year by the Greek Orthodox patriarch and the Roman Catholic cardinal of Jerusalem.

It is also home to the Taybeh Brewing Co, widely considered the Middle East's oldest microbrewery.

Some Western ​countries have ​announced sanctions on settler groups over violent ​Israeli attacks on Palestinians.

In June, Israeli ‌settlers obstructed Palestinians putting out a large blaze near Taybeh in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian civil defence firefighters and a local priest who described an "ongoing pattern of intimidation and unjustified violence" that undermined the residents' fundamental rights.

A U.N. inquiry released on Tuesday found that Israeli authorities were directly involved in settler attacks that ‌have killed, injured and displaced Palestinians in the ​West Bank. The Israeli mission in Geneva rejected ​the report's findings, saying Israeli authorities ​including the president and prime minister had repeatedly condemned violence against ‌Palestinians.

Parts of Taybeh are located in ​Area B, where the ​Palestinian Authority runs civil administration but where security control must be coordinated with Israeli authorities.

The West Bank and Jerusalem are home to around 50,000 Palestinian Christians, ​members of a religious ‌community there stretching back to antiquity in a region that is home ​to many of the faith's most important holy sites.

title: Biden-world veteran issues stark warning about Abdul El-Sayed as he crosses party lines

fullText:
Former Jill Biden press secretary Michael LaRosa said he won't support Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, citing the candidate's refusal to distance himself from far-left streamer Hasan Piker over his past remarks about the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.

LaRosa, who served as press secretary to former first lady Jill Biden, made the unusually sharp break with his party in a post responding to reports that he was supporting Republican Mike Rogers over El-Sayed.

At the center of LaRosa's criticism is El-Sayed's association with Piker, who drew widespread condemnation after saying during a 2019 livestream that "America deserved 9/11."

El-sayed's Socialist Allies Reject Gop Claims About Dems Embracing The Far Left

El-Sayed has campaigned alongside Piker and, when pressed about the remark, has argued that appearing with the streamer does not mean he endorses everything Piker has said.

For LaRosa, the controversy is deeply personal. He said the mother of his best friend died on Sept. 11 after jumping from the 95th floor of the World Trade Center rather than remain inside the burning building.

"I won't defend or support anyone who is too cowardly to stand up to extremists who think the mother of my best friend, who jumped from 95 stories because the alternative was worse, deserved what happened to her," LaRosa wrote. "Her only crime was showing up to work that morning."

Hasan Piker Calls For Democrats Who Oppose Abdul El-sayed To Be 'Punished'

LaRosa concluded by accusing El-Sayed of refusing to stand up to "the guy who says she 'deserved' what she got that morning she showed up for work."

LaRosa's rebuke is about more than one Democrat refusing to back another.

It highlights a growing fault line within the party over extremism and the boundaries of acceptable political rhetoric. Those divisions could ultimately push some longtime Democrats across the aisle in consequential races.

That dynamic could prove particularly consequential in Michigan, where the Senate contest could help shape the balance of power in Washington and even a small erosion of Democratic support could matter.
