title: Ocasio-Cortez declines to endorse Hong, says she’s focused on ‘winning back’ Congress
description: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) on Sunday declined to endorse Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist vying for the party nomination in the Wisconsin governor’s race. “I haven’t endorsed in that...
fullText:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) on Sunday declined to endorse Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist vying for the party nomination in the Wisconsin governor's race.

"I haven't endorsed in that race. My focus has been in winning back the Congress, winning back the House and positioning ourselves to have the best chance possible to win the Senate," Ocasio-Cortez said during an appearance on ABC News's "This Week."

Her decision falls in line with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and the national branch of the Democratic Socialists of America, which have both declined to endorse Hong.

In previous years, Hong shared statements in support of abolishing prisons, defunding the police and canceling Thanksgiving, all of which are views the gubernatorial candidate says have now shifted.

"I think that a lot of these races, even right now, they'll have a tendency to be nationalized. But these races ultimately are local, and all politics are local. My understanding is that Francesca Hong has made clear her presence in her election," Ocasio-Cortez said in response to questions about Hong's views.

"She's moved away from it," she added.

Host Jonathan Karl asked the New York representative about where she now stands in regard to defunding the police, which is a crime solution she previously amplified.

"I think that during this time and … especially during COVID, there was a huge opening of the overtone window. We were shut down. There was some of the highest unemployment rates that we have seen because of those shutdowns, and I think that the doors were really open in trying to entertain any and every policy that was going to get us to a better place, and I actually think that the discussions … that were had in that time were quite fruitful," Ocasio-Cortez said.

"I think that when we talk about crime today, it's fundamentally different than the way that we talked about crime in bringing crime down, right? And I think that we all share the goals of having as low a crime rate as possible," she continued.

Ocasio-Cortez added that rhetoric used during lockdown, "is not rhetoric that we would use today."

"And I'm grateful that these candidates have the opportunity to present who they are to their electorate and what they're campaigning on in this moment," she added.

title: The Trump admin offered sick Medicaid patients a 1-year lifeline. These red states are rejecting it.
description: Several conservative states will require proof from people who say they're too sick to work.
fullText:
Democrats say the Trump administration's new Medicaid work requirements — especially the narrow definition of who can get an exemption for medical reasons — are way too harsh.

Conservatives contend they're not tough enough, and have convinced some Republican-led states to be even stricter.

The federal government gave states the option of allowing people to stay on Medicaid through 2027 if they declare themselves too sick to work, with verification starting in 2028. But at least eight states are rejecting that grace period and demanding proof earlier. Starting in January, Arkansas, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, and Utah will impose work rules stricter than those the administration is requiring.

Their decision underscores many conservatives' belief that the expansion of Medicaid under Obamacare covered too many people that they consider unworthy of support, such as non-disabled, working-age adults without children. Democrats and advocates for low-income people say the harsher enforcement will cause many more sick people to join the ranks of the uninsured faster, putting the burden of caring for them on already-strained emergency rooms and public health clinics.

The policies adopted by the eight GOP-leaning states are the culmination of a massive lobbying campaign by conservative organizations who view the administration's decision to forgo verification of medical frailty next year as a "loophole" that people will exploit to get out of working.

Jonathan Ingram, the vice president of policy and research at the Foundation for Government Accountability, a conservative think tank and advocacy group, said in an interview that his organization spent the last year deploying lobbyists and "encouraging lawmakers across the country" to pass bills requiring Medicaid recipients to prove they're too sick to work starting next year, and imposing other "strong guardrails…. so agency bureaucrats can't come in and undermine the work that Congress did."

Several states did adopt such legislation — over the objections of Democratic lawmakers. In others, the move towards tougher enforcement came from the health department.

"They sprung into action to put in as many impediments as possible to people remaining on Medicaid," said Idaho Democratic Rep. Ilana Rubel, the minority leader in the statehouse who argued against the bill requiring strict enforcement of the work requirement, which the governor signed into law earlier this year. "We're already lowest in the nation per capita for health care providers, and I think it will get substantially worse when they finally attain their dream of kicking tens of thousands more people off of their health insurance."

The new work rules stem from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Republicans in Congress passed last year requiring Medicaid enrollees to work, volunteer or study at least 80 hours per month. The policy applies to the 21 million or so people who gained eligibility for Medicaid through Obamacare, and nonpartisan analysts expected it to drive up the number of people who lose Medicaid by at least 5 million over a decade.

An analysis by the health consulting firm Manatt of states that previously enacted their own Medicaid work rules found that states that allowed patients to retain coverage if they claimed to have a serious medical condition — a practice called "self-attestation" — saw far fewer people lose their coverage.

Arkansas granted exemptions to its state work requirement when patients said they were too sick to work, and saw around 29 percent of its Medicaid patients lose coverage. Yet in New Hampshire, which only allowed parents of young children and other narrow categories to claim such an exemption without state verification, more than 40 percent were projected to lose coverage before a court ruling blocked the policy from taking effect.

Health policy experts stress that eligible people are still likely to lose coverage in the majority of states that are planning to allow patients to cite an illness to get an exemption from the work requirement — either because they are unaware of the option or unable to navigate the bureaucracy.

"Requiring individuals to go get documentation from their provider to demonstrate their medical frailty is going to place such a significant burden on people to make the appointment, to obtain the documentation, to put the stress on the provider, to make that assessment," said Kinda Serafi, a partner at Manatt Health. "People who live in rural areas, people who live in states that have provider shortages, or there's a lack of transportation, are going to really struggle to document medical frailty, even if they clearly qualify."

The Foundation for Government Accountability, whose work has been funded by the Koch family and other GOP megadonors, has spent more than a decade pushing states to restrict access to the social safety net. In the last few years, its lobbyists worked to convince legislatures to make it harder for people to access SNAP, Medicaid and other public benefit programs.

Over the last year, the group contracted with lobbyists in Idaho, Indiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, North Carolina, and Utah to push lawmakers to enact legislation to implement strict Medicaid work requirements — with provisions that go beyond the parameters set by the Trump administration.

In particular, the group urged state lawmakers to turn down the federal government's offer of a one-year grace period that allows patients to sign a sworn statement under penalty of perjury that they are medically frail without having to provide a doctor's note or other evidence.

"We've recommended it to any state that will listen to us," said Ingram. "We are trying to preach the gospel of work and the value of work."

Ingram pointed to the implementation of work requirements for the SNAP food program in 1996 as a cautionary tale, lamenting that blue states "went after as many exemptions and waivers as possible."

Now the group is eyeing Medicaid.

"We've seen audit after audit that shows if you are not verifying what people tell you then you are getting a lot of people who are ineligible," he said. "We view that as essentially fraud by design. These are policies designed by bureaucrats to allow essentially legalized fraud."

In many places, the group's call for tougher enforcement met a receptive audience. Many state and federal Republicans argue that strict work requirements are needed because Medicaid spending growth in recent years — more than double the rate of inflation — has put the program on unstable footing.

The federal government pays the bulk of Medicaid expansion costs, but states manage the programs individually. Removing people who can't prove they are either working or sick, conservatives contend, will help ensure coverage for the single parents and disabled people the program served before Obamacare.

North Carolina's Republican-controlled legislature passed a bill earlier this year that prohibits state and county officials "from accepting self-attestation as the only evidence in verification of Medicaid eligibility requirements, including new Medicaid work requirements," the state's health department confirmed in a statement to POLITICO.

"North Carolina has done what is necessary to comply with federal laws while focusing anew on wasteful spending, fraud and abuse in health care," said Republican Rep. Donny Lambeth, who voted in favor of expanding Medicaid in 2023. "We are just complying with federal laws while working with the counties to help them lower their eligibility error rates."

While several states claimed an ideological or fiscal motivation for demanding proof of illness earlier than the Trump administration mandated, others said they were doing so to avoid confusion that may result from having one policy in 2027 and another in 2028.

"A consistent verification process also ensures a tracking record for future reviews," North Dakota's Medicaid agency said in a statement.

Iowa's health department echoed that rationale, telling POLITICO it will use "a single, standardized process to provide clarity for both members and eligibility workers."

In Idaho, under a law the legislature passed overwhelmingly this spring, new Medicaid patients can claim an exemption for medical frailty for the first six months of the work rules, but will have to show proof when their coverage is renewed and when the state conducts eligibility checks every six months after that.

Rubel, the Idaho Democrat, is worried that proof of illness will be hard to come by for her Boise constituents due to doctor shortages in the area.

"I have private health insurance, and I'm regularly told it's a six-to-eight month waiting list," she said.

Ohio's Medicaid agency is confronting similar challenges as it joins the cadre of states rejecting the Trump administration's one-year grace period. Its Medicaid agency told POLITICO it is working with federal health officials to come up with a solution for medically frail people newly enrolling in Medicaid who do not have access to a doctor and aren't able to obtain an examination and diagnosis.

"We're falling into the idea that health care is a privilege. It's just horrible," said Anita Somani, a Democrat and OB/GYN who represents the Columbus area in the Ohio legislature. "And we're already seeing the real world consequences in our medical practices. People are canceling surgeries. They're rationing their meds because they can't fill the prescription until their next paycheck."

What kind of documentation to require of sick patients on Medicaid is a conundrum facing many states as the 2027 implementation deadline draws near.

Hilarie Matlock, the policy director for the advocacy group Idaho Voices for Children, said uninsured sick people will face a Catch-22: they can't get Medicaid without first seeing a doctor to get proof of their condition, but they can't afford to see a doctor without insurance.

Self-attestation, she noted, has long been accepted in Medicaid for things such as income, and she disagrees with conservative advocates who view it as a loophole.

"It is not simply taking a person's word for it," said Matlock. "It is a sworn statement made under penalty of perjury."

title: How Liverpool are shaping up under Iraola
description: Four pre-season games is a very small sample, but Andoni Iraola is starting to put his stamp on Liverpool. So how are the Reds shaping up under their new boss?
fullText:
Winning is important - but for many fans, how a team plays in the hunt for wins is almost as significant.

When results don't come, a style that fans enjoy watching often buys a manager more time than a pragmatist might be afforded.

Andoni Iraola replaced Arne Slot as Liverpool head coach a season after the latter won the Premier League with the Reds.

Many believe the Spanish coach's style is more aligned with the 'heavy metal' style of football Anfield had come to love under Jurgen Klopp.

So how have Liverpool fared in their pre-season games so far under Iraola?

Liverpool have beaten Sunderland and Wrexham in pre-season, but they threw away two-goal leads in defeats by both Leeds and Monaco.

They averaged 60.6% possession over this small sample size - which is a 12.9% jump on Bournemouth's average possession under Iraola in the league last season.

With teams more likely to sit deep against Liverpool, having lots of possession is a newer challenge Iraola has to tackle.

And he has looked to do this while sticking to the intense and chaotic style that typified his previous sides.

Follow Liverpool to get live score updates this season

Since joining Liverpool, many of Iraola's tactics in possession look as they did last season.

Liverpool have looked to build up short at times with their goalkeeper, four defenders and one or two central midfielders deep.

Dominik Szoboszlai and Trey Nyoni, Liverpool's preferred deeper midfield duo in pre-season, drop to show for the ball, bouncing it towards wide players in space.

Iraola's sides have become known for fast and vertical counter-attacks but, with Liverpool looking to hold the ball more deliberately, these short passes in build-up are designed to entice opposition pressure before accelerating play.

Once a team have committed players to pressing Liverpool, Iraola's men look for forward passes readily - almost manufacturing their own counter-attacks.

If a team press immediately, Liverpool have been willing to skip short build-up play and go long from keepers Alisson or Giorgi Mamardashvili early.

Many of Iraola's attacking principles resemble those of one of his long-time managerial inspirations, the former Leeds United boss Marcelo Bielsa.

The Argentine coached Iraola at Athletic Club between 2011 and 2013 and, speaking to Sky Sports in 2023, the Liverpool boss acknowledged this influence.

"I use a lot of exercises from Marcelo that I learned from him, especially with the ball," Iraola said.

"Offensively, his teams are very dynamic, willing to make all the runs to the space, he is ready to accept this kind of disorder offensively."

Like Bielsa's sides, Iraola already has the Reds playing in a busy manner. When attacking, it is rare to see Liverpool's players filling specific areas in a rigid style.

Another tactic Bielsa leans on is the use of wide pairings or trios to break teams down. Iraola experienced this at first hand when playing as a right-back for him.

The full-back and winger would regularly combine on the outside, but the relationship was never as simple as one holding the width and the other supporting underneath statically.

Bielsa, like Iraola now, encouraged players to change their positions in relation to each other.

The winger could come inside, opening the outside lane for the full-back, while a midfielder would move towards the pair to create a third passing option.

On other occasions, the full-back could move inside himself, allowing the winger to remain high and wide.

Liverpool are already showing similar patterns under Iraola, especially on the left, where full-backs have pushed into the final third alongside Rio Ngumoha or Cody Gakpo on the left wing.

Florian Wirtz, playing primarily as Liverpool's number 10 under Iraola, has drifted to that flank to provide a third option capable of playing centrally, deep or out wide.

The rotations of these wide triangles make it hard for opponents to know who they should be picking up.

As exciting as this style of play can appear, it does leave Liverpool very top-heavy.

In the opening games, we have seen both full-backs join the attack alongside two of the midfield three and the front three.

This can result in situations that leave only the two centre-backs and one holding midfielder positioned behind the ball, leaving Liverpool vulnerable to counter-attacks.

Interestingly, Slot’s Liverpool were noticeably vulnerable against fast counter-attacks last season too.

Iraola has spoken about the need for more control while retaining the chaos that makes his team's attacks so effective, so he may decide to leave additional players behind the ball as the season progresses.

However, based off his previous principles and his managerial references, this feels less likely - with the Basque coach often encouraging six or seven players to push forward, leaving three or four players back when in attack.

The hope is to stop counter-attacks being conceded at source through intense counter-presses, something that is helped by attacking down the sides and with extra bodies nearby to apply pressure.

This is easier said than done at this early stage.

Indeed, Iraola reflected on the loss to Monaco, saying his side "can't sustain the level we want, we have work to do", referring to the dropped leads in second halves, caused by a lack of depth, a drop-off in physicality, and a press that hasn't yet been perfected.

Throughout pre-season, we have also seen Iraola's trademark high press. What stands out is the roles Liverpool's players are taking up and what that tells us about how he wants his side to defend.

Szoboszlai played across the front line, midfield and even at right-back last season, but Iraola has mainly used him as the second central midfielder - a crucial role defensively.

Liverpool have often pressed in a 4-4-2 diamond shape, initially encouraging opponents to play short before launching more aggressive pressing sequences, often funnelling the ball centrally before trying to win it back.

One principle carried over from Iraola's Bournemouth side is looking to keep a spare defender against the opposition attack. If an opponent leaves three forwards high, Liverpool will commonly opt to keep four defenders back.

That leaves one fewer player higher up the pitch, so Liverpool have to compensate through intensity and intelligent covering.

When one player leaves his opponent to press somebody else, team-mates behind him have to recognise the movement and cover the player left free.

This makes Szoboszlai's midfield role particularly important. When he jumps forward to press, the holding midfielder and defensive line have to react behind him or gaps can quickly appear.

"He is very good," the Hungary captain has said of his new manager. "The intensity we need is here now, what we have been missing is back."

Szoboszlai's physicality allows him to cover the ground needed to make Liverpool's press feel numerically equal, while his judgement of when to step forward has helped the Reds start to implement Iraola's defensive ideas quickly.

Four pre-season games is a very small sample, but Iraola's stamp on Liverpool is already clear to see, featuring many of the same instructions that defined his Bournemouth side.

Those ideas have been proven to work - but how he balances the chaos and speed we've come to know his sides for, with a squad lacking depth and who are expected to dominate the ball for longer periods, is likely to shape his first season.

title: The Argentine who wishes he could play for Wales
description: Proud of his Welsh roots, Chile-based Argentine defender Jeremias James hopes for a rule change to help his international ambitions.
fullText:
There has been a small slice of Wales in Argentina for more than 150 years.

About 160 Welsh emigrants sailed to Patagonia in 1865 to create a new settlement, 'Y Wladfa', where their language, culture and religion could flourish free from English influence and dominance.

The language is still actively spoken there, while more than 50,000 Patagonians can claim Welsh ancestry.

One of those is Jeremias James.

James was born and raised in Trelew, a city founded in 1886 by Welsh settlers in the Chubut province.

Its name translates from Welsh to "Town of Lewis" in honour of its founder, Lewis Jones.

"I'm part of a Welsh family, a Welsh colony that settled in southern Argentina, specifically in Chubut," James told BBC Sport Wales.

"Five generations of my family were born in Trelew, and I'm part of the the fifth generation.

"Over the years my family settled in Chubut and that's where my story, my family, and all my descendants come from."

After the first journey across the Atlantic Ocean to Patagonia in 1865, more followed over the next few years.

Many Welsh immigrants in 19th-century North America later joined the South American settlement to help sustain the Welsh-speaking community.

After the initial settlement in the Chubut Valley proved difficult, additional groups arrived not only from Wales, but also from established Welsh farming communities in the USA.

"Looking into my family's history the first member to travel to Patagonia was William James on a ship from the United States," added Jeremias.

"David Stephen James was the first member of the family born in Argentina, and that would be my great-great-grandfather.

"Then came my great-grandfather, my grandfather, my father, and me. All born in Trelew.

"The land in Chubut was granted to Welsh settlers, and my family still live there today. That land belongs to us."

Beyond his Welsh heritage, James has a powerful personal story.

At the age of nine he was diagnosed with leukemia and had to move to Buenos Aires for treatment.

"I was on that treatment for about a year or two until I returned to Trelew, discharged, and gradually resumed my normal life," he said.

After recovering he played for youth teams in Chubut before being scouted by San Lorenzo's academy, one of Argentine football's biggest clubs who are based in Buenos Aires.

After making his debut for San Lorenzo in Argentina's Primera Division in 2022, he spent time on loan at Barracas Central, Deportivo Riestra and Alvarado, all based in his home country.

The 25-year-old currently plays for Primera B side Magallanes in Chile, joining them on a permanent basis earlier this year after a successful loan spell.

Even though his family have strong Welsh roots, it is unlikely James will ever be able to play for Wales.

FIFA rules dictate that a player's biological parents or grandparents must have been born in the country they wish to represent.

But even though the current footballing eligibility rules do not work in James' favour, he is eager to find out more about his heritage.

"I was born and raised in Argentina, but obviously I've always been aware of my connection to Wales," said James.

"As you progress and develop in this sport, you always consider the possibility of playing for a national team you have family connections with.

"First of all I would love to visit the country. I haven't had the chance to travel to Wales, and it's something I'd really like to experience to find out more about my roots and where my family comes from.

"It's a dream of mine, and one that I'll surely be able to fulfil someday.

"But of course if the opportunity arises to play in that country, whether for the national team or for a club, it would be something truly very special for me."

A left-footed, ball-playing central defender, James is also strong in the air.

He has been a regular in the Magallanes team this season as they aim to win promotion back to the top flight in Chile.

"I've always been a central defender, and I've always enjoyed playing there," James explained.

"I see my strengths as being a good leader on the pitch and my aerial play.

"We've been lucky in Argentina over the past few years that we've had a very good national team and great defenders.

"I've always admired players like Cristian Romero and Nicolas Otamendi. I've followed their careers closely and tried to emulate what they do on the pitch."

It does not seem likely James will be able to play on the international stage like his heroes.

But rules can change in football, and if that ever happens, it would certainly be welcomed by the Chubut community in Patagonia.

title: Indian national accused of Arizona girlfriend's murder entered US on student visa: federal sources
description: Varun Batchigari allegedly strangled Julissa Salazar near the University of Arizona, then boarded a flight to India before the FBI had him arrested.
fullText:
The man accused of murdering his teenage girlfriend in Arizona allegedly tried to cover his tracks, flee the country and vanish overseas.

Federal law enforcement sources told Fox News the accused killer, 20-year-old Varun Batchigari, is an Indian national who entered the United States through Los Angeles International Airport on Jan. 8, 2024, on an F-1 student visa.

After the alleged killing, authorities say Batchigari boarded a flight from Houston bound for India with a layover in Germany, where he was arrested after the FBI alerted local authorities.

Migrant Who Fled Ireland After American Mother's Murder Is Arrested In Jordan

The FBI is now working to extradite him back to Arizona to face a first-degree murder charge.

Batchigari is charged with murdering his 19-year-old girlfriend, Julissa Salazar, who Tucson police say was strangled Thursday inside an off-campus apartment near the University of Arizona.

Investigators allege Batchigari stole Salazar's cellphone and credit cards after the killing, then sent a series of text messages to her mother while posing as the victim in an apparent attempt to conceal the crime. The messages raised concern among Salazar's family, prompting a welfare check that led officers to discover her body.

A felony warrant paints a picture of escalating violence, a deteriorating relationship and mounting personal troubles in the months leading up to Salazar's death.

Fitness Trainer Told Friend She Was 'Scared For Her Life' Weeks Before Body With Matching Clothing Found

According to the warrant, obtained by KOLD-TV, Batchigari had previously been involved in an assault case investigated by the University of Arizona Police Department.

Witnesses interviewed by investigators said Salazar moved out after experiencing problems with Batchigari in late 2025 and had planned to end the relationship because of an alleged history of domestic violence.

The warrant also includes allegations from multiple witnesses describing prior violent behavior. One witness told investigators Batchigari sexually assaulted her at a Halloween party but said she never reported the allegation to law enforcement.

Another witness told investigators Batchigari had been expelled from the University of Arizona following a fight and later lost his job, leading to financial problems and concerns about his student visa status and ability to pay rent.

Exclusive: Dhs Seeks Custody Of Illegal Immigrant Charged With Murder After Trump Deportation, Biden Release

Federal records reviewed by Fox News show Batchigari remained in lawful immigration status at the time of the alleged murder despite his reported expulsion from the University of Arizona.

Because international students on F-1 visas are generally required to remain enrolled to maintain their legal status, it is unclear why his immigration status had not yet changed.

A Tucson Police Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital there were no updates beyond the information already released publicly. Fox News Digital also reached out to the University of Arizona to confirm Batchigari's enrollment history and whether Salazar was a student, but did not immediately receive a response.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Talarico caught on tape giggling about his church housing illegal immigrants set for deportation
description: James Talarico bragged his church housed an undocumented family facing ICE deportation, saying Christianity is "just another word for causing trouble."
fullText:
EXCLUSIVE: Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico bragged in a resurfaced interview that his church had stirred controversy by housing a family of illegal immigrants who were set to be deported by ICE, laughing as he said that "Christianity is just another word for causing trouble."

Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian who serves as a Democratic state representative, is running against Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton for a Senate seat that is critical to both parties.

In a resurfaced clip of Talarico speaking on Texas Impact's "Weekly Witness" show in June 2023, he credited his faith for "why I am in politics." Asked how his faith influences his politics, Talarico pointed to examples of his church advancing progressive causes, saying, "Justice is just love out in public."

"Our church was really active in LGBTQ rights in the '90s. We caught some attention by letting an atheist join our church in the 2000s, and then in the 2010s, again stirred some controversy by housing an undocumented family, a mother and son, who were close to being deported by ICE," he said. "That was the tradition that I was brought up in. It's what led me to teach public school students on the west side of San Antonio, led me to run an education nonprofit and then led me to run for office."

Texas Dem Nominee James Talarico Invokes Faith To Defend Abortion Rights, 'The Bible Is Silent On Abortion'

"And so, again," he continued, "this idea that Christianity is just another word for causing trouble."

During the same interview, Talarico decried what he referred to as "Christo-fascism" and the religious right, which he accused of seeking to subvert democracy by forcing a "certain type of Christianity."

Asked for specific examples of Christo-fascism in Texas, he pointed to a law requiring public schools to display the Ten Commandments, another allowing schools to replace guidance counselors with chaplains, and the state's school voucher program. He also pointed to laws banning sex-change surgeries and treatments for children and Texas' abortion ban.

"All these ideologies stem from this Christo-fascism movement, which, essentially, like I said, is just using faith to exercise raw political, social and economic power," said Talarico. "I think it's dangerous to all of us, but particularly to those who are marginalized and oppressed in our state."

Socialist House Nominee's Radical Law-and-order Vision: 'What Are Illegals?'

The resurfaced clip has drawn criticism from Republicans.

Republican National Committee spokesman Zach Kraft told Fox News Digital that "despite looking like a loser, Talarico is a dangerous man."

"He has dedicated his life to helping illegals by dismantling border security, defunding police, and abolishing prisons to turn Texas into a paradise for cartels and criminals," said Kraft.

JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico's campaign, responded by telling Fox News Digital that "James is a Christian seminarian who's dedicated his life to the teachings of Jesus Christ — fighting religious and political corruption when he sees it because there's nothing Christ-like about powerful people twisting the teachings of Jesus to justify hate, violence, and greed. While billionaire-bought politicians like Ken Paxton attack James for his faith — he will continue encouraging Texans across the political spectrum to come together by loving their neighbors as themselves."

Ennis said that the RNC's "attacks are flat out lies."

"James opposes defunding the police and supports stronger border security and immigration enforcement — it's why he's voted to send billions of dollars to support law enforcement, called for more border patrol agents, and has said we should be arresting and deporting violent criminals and human traffickers — not moms and babies," said Ennis. "On the other hand, Ken Paxton's fellow Republicans have blasted his record of abusing his office to benefit his wealthy donors and the well-connected, allowing criminals back on the street even as it made Texans less safe."

The Democratic National Committee did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Despite Republican efforts to highlight his history of controversial statements, including saying that "God is nonbinary" and that there are six sexes, Talarico leads Paxton in a recent Fox News poll.

Republicans, including Paxton, argue that Talarico's progressive record will eventually hurt him politically.

Dem's Stunning Ideal Standard For Immigration Detention Conditions Resurfaces Amid Texas Senate Bid

Madison Cercy, a spokeswoman for Paxton's campaign, commented on the resurfaced video, telling Fox News Digital that "In Talarico's form of Christianity, you must be trans, you can't support the oil and gas industry, you must support late-term abortions, and you have to let in every criminal illegal immigrant seeking asylum."

"James Talarico hates Christianity, and he's said it," added Cercy. "The only form of Christianity Talarico practices is one that sacrifices children at the altar of the radical trans movement and most Texans would agree."

Paxton told Fox News Digital after a rally in Houston earlier this week that Talarico's lead is "not surprising" given "we were three months behind" after his primary runoff against incumbent Sen. John Cornyn.

"We're still three months out," Paxton continued. "And I know that when we put our resources together, when we get there, we will be able to highlight things and once the voters know the real James Talarico, not the fake one that's running right now … people will get to decide for themselves."

title: Syria will take back control from Russia of 2 key Mediterranean bases under a new deal
description: Russian forces in Syria will give up control of two strategic bases on the Mediterranean coast, which will be used as joint Russia-Syrian training centers under a new agreement between the two countri...
fullText:
DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — Russian forces in Syria will give up control of two strategic bases on the Mediterranean coast, which will be used as joint Russia-Syrian training centers under a new agreement between the two countries, Syria's Foreign Ministry said Sunday.

Russia was the top political and military ally of ousted President Bashar Assad during the country's civil war between 2011 and 2024. Assad was ousted in December 2024 by Islamist insurgents led by current interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa and has since fled into exile in Russia.

Throughout the conflict, the Hmeimem air base and the Tartus naval base were key Russian military outposts in the eastern Mediterranean.

Under the new agreement between Damascus and Moscow, Syria will take control of the Hmeimem air base and the commercial berth at Tartus port as part of its civil administration. The military facilities at both sites will become "joint training" centers, the Foreign Ministry said.

The new arrangements represent a "reorganizing of the Russian presence" along Syria's coast, the ministry said.

"This move marks the most significant development since negotiations began approximately a year and a half ago, paving the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations," the statement read.

Russia did not immediately comment on the agreement.

Moscow did not interfere during the lightning insurgency that led to Assad's overthrow, but it provided the longtime Syrian leader and his family asylum. After Assad's ouster Russian troops remaining in Syria gradually left the country except for those stationed at the bases.

Syria's new leadership has aimed to maintain strong bilateral ties with Moscow. Al-Sharaa has visited President Vladimir Putin in Moscow twice since taking power, with the two Mediterranean bases being key points of discussion.

Since Assad's ouster, Syria has also bolstered its ties with the United States, Europe, and neighboring Arab countries that had cut ties with Damascus during Assad's crackdown on protests. Washington has lifted most of its crippling sanctions on the country, and French President Emmanuel Macron made a visit to Syria in July during which he announced that the two countries would appoint respective ambassadors for the first time in 14 years.

title: By propping up the yen, the U.S. and Japan are actually admitting dollar dominance isn’t what it used to be, top economist warns
description: "When this message sinks in, other countries will redouble their search for more attractive, readily usable alternatives."
fullText:
Last week's attempt to boost the sagging yen wasn't the first time the U.S. and Japan took such joint action, but the way they did it revealed weakness in the dollar's global status, according to a top currency expert.

In a Financial Times op-ed on Tuesday, University of California at Berkeley economist Barry Eichengreen pointed to both sides of the currency intervention, which he said reflected concern about long-term yields going up.

On the U.S. end, the New York Fed sold euros instead of dollar-denominated assets to buy yen. Eichengreen said that allowed the U.S. to avoid calling on financial markets to absorb more Treasury securities.

That's as the federal government must finance a $2 trillion budget deficit this fiscal year, meaning it's already issuing a flood of Treasury debt. Meanwhile, it's also competing against AI hyperscalers who are selling a mountain of their own bonds.

The tsunami of public and private debt as well as the competition for investor demand have put upward pressure on yields, which adds to interest costs and the federal deficit.

On the Japanese side of the intervention, Tokyo also refrained from selling Treasuries and instead tapped an obscure Federal Reserve tool called the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility.

This mechanism allowed Japan, which is the world's largest holder of U.S. debt, to borrow dollars against its Treasury stockpile, obtaining a limited form of liquidity.

"Both moves are an indication that the dollar's status as a reserve currency is not what it used to be," Eichengreen wrote. "Central banks are accustomed to holding foreign reserves in dollars because markets in U.S. Treasury securities are liquid. Central banks hold U.S. Treasuries because they can be freely bought and sold and used in interventions. But not now, at least not in unlimited quantities."

That's strikes at the heart of dollar dominance, which is in part derived from the immense size and depth of the U.S. debt market.

But by signaling that Treasuries can't be used anytime and anywhere, the U.S. gives investors less of a reason to own them.

"The bottom line is that Washington, fearing the consequences for U.S. financial markets, is reluctant to see foreign central banks use their dollar reserves," Eichengreen concluded. "This is telling us that the dollar is not the attractive reserve currency it once was. When this message sinks in, other countries will redouble their search for more attractive, readily usable alternatives."

Kieran Tompkins, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, echoed that sentiment, saying in a note on Friday that the U.S. is raising the relative appeal of holding assets like gold because it pressured Japan to not sell dollar assets.

title: Hawaii contractor nominated to construct GOP comeback after two-decade Democratic hold on governor's mansion
description: Gary Cordery won the Republican nomination for Hawaii governor and now faces Democratic Gov. Josh Green despite a massive fundraising gap ahead.
fullText:
Gary Cordery, who owns a contracting company, won the Republican nomination for Hawaii governor after defeating business owner Ken Fujiyama in Saturday's primary.

He is now set to face Democratic Gov. Josh Green in November in a race that heavily favors the incumbent. The Cook Political Report rates the contest as Solid Democratic, with a Partisan Voting Index of D+13.

Cordery faces a steep challenge: Hawaii has not had a Republican governor since Linda Lingle left office in 2010.

Former Top Oregon Gop Official Secures Nomination For Governor As Republicans Target Blue-state Pickup

In addition to facing an incumbent with a 56% approval rating and Hawaii's long history of Democratic control, Cordery faces a significant financial disadvantage against Green.

Green has raised approximately $3.5 million, far outpacing Cordery, who has raised about $313,000, according to Honolulu Civil Beat.

Despite the uphill battle, Cordery is pitching voters on a platform centered on lowering Hawaii's high cost of living, reforming education and cracking down on corruption.

"As a husband, father and grandfather, businessman and community servant, I love Hawai'i," Cordery said in an interview with Honolulu Civil Beat. "These islands of unique beauty have endured mismanagement for decades. Her people live under tremendous stress and anxiety. I am running to open opportunity, create abundance and ensure stewardship of her resources, bringing accountability and hope for the people."

The American Dream Now Comes With A Zip Code: Here's Where Starter Homes Are Still Within Reach

Part of Cordery's plan to create abundance includes adding 15,000 homes across the islands for working families, with prices ranging from roughly $400,000 to $600,000. His proposal calls for using state-owned land for fee-simple housing while streamlining permitting and opening more land for residential development.

He is also proposing eliminating the state's General Excise Tax on food and medicine and freezing property taxes for homeowners at retirement. Cordery argues that the state is failing to properly manage taxpayers' dollars and says he would order audits to root out waste.

"Hawai'i's 20.5 billion dollar budget for 1.4 mil[lion] people is a staggering number. New Hampshire has 1.4 million people but a $7.75 billion dollar budget," Cordery said. "I believe our tax burden is out of control. The answer is management."

title: Why NHL Forward Noah Philp Walked Away From Hockey at Just 27 Years Old
description: A promising center retires weeks after signing a new contract, revealing a deeper struggle few saw coming.
fullText:
Professional hockey has lost a player whose journey was anything but conventional. Just weeks after putting pen to paper on a deal with Swedish Hockey League club HV71, a 27-year-old forward shocked the hockey world by announcing his permanent retirement from the sport. The timing caught many off guard, but the signs had been there for years.

Noah Philp was never selected in the NHL Draft, yet he managed to carve out a path to the highest level of the sport through sheer determination and skill. After lighting up the WHL as a prolific scorer with the Seattle Thunderbirds, Philp attended the University of Alberta before turning professional in the spring of 2022 with the Edmonton Oilers organization. His rookie campaign with the Bakersfield Condors in the AHL during the 2022-2023 season was impressive, tallying 37 points across 70 games and establishing himself as a genuine development success story.

However, it was precisely at that juncture that Philp's trajectory took an unexpected turn. Instead of building on his momentum and pushing for a full-time NHL roster spot, the 6-foot-3 center stepped away from the game entirely for a full season. That initial departure hinted that thoughts of retirement were already swirling in his mind far earlier than they do for most professional athletes.

When he returned for the 2024-2025 campaign, Philp picked up right where he left off, posting 35 points in 55 AHL contests and earning his first NHL call-up. He appeared in 15 games with the Oilers. The following season, he earned a spot on Edmonton's roster out of training camp but managed only three points in 15 games before being placed on waivers in early December. The Carolina Hurricanes claimed him off the wire, though his time in Carolina at the NHL level was fleeting, consisting of just two games. He spent the remainder of the season in the AHL with the Chicago Wolves, where he was outstanding during the playoffs, recording 14 points in 21 postseason games as the team advanced all the way to the Calder Cup Final.

In a statement released through HV71, Philp apologized to the Swedish club for the awkward timing of his announcement. He had only recently signed a one-year contract that included an option for a second season. Despite the unfortunate circumstances, Philp chose transparency over pretense, explaining that his motivation for hockey was no longer fully there. Rather than go through the motions and fail to give his all on the ice, he felt it was more respectful to be upfront about where he stood mentally.

HV71 acknowledged the situation and confirmed they would move quickly to find a replacement to fill the gap in their lineup. The club's measured response underscored a mutual respect between player and organization, even in a difficult moment.

Philp's retirement closes the book on a career that, while relatively brief, was genuinely inspiring in its arc from undrafted college player to NHL regular. His story serves as a powerful reminder that talent and opportunity alone do not sustain a career at the professional level. The human element, particularly internal drive and personal fulfillment, plays an equally critical role. For Philp, stepping away was not a sign of weakness but an act of self-awareness that few athletes are willing to embrace so openly.

title: Can Oklahoma Make The College Football Playoff With A 9-3 Record? Paul Finebaum Thinks So...
description: The ESPN host claims the Sooners' brutal SEC gauntlet offers a rare lifeline, potentially rewarding a three-loss campaign with an unprecedented invitation to the expanded postseason
fullText:
Paul Finebaum isn't usually one to hand out easy paths, but he recently put Oklahoma in a small group of teams that could still reach the College Football Playoff even with three losses.

Speaking on The Paul Finebaum Show on ESPN Radio and the SEC Network, he laid it out clearly. "There are a couple of teams that would have a really good shot at making it at 9-3," Finebaum said. "Texas would be one. Oklahoma would be another. To get in with three losses, you better have played a significant schedule and nonconference. I think those are the two. LSU, probably because of playing Clemson."

Finebaum is acknowledging both the strength of Oklahoma's schedule and the reality of how the expanded playoff works. A tough slate can create a path that softer schedules simply don't have.

Still, history shows how difficult that path actually is.

No 9-3 team has ever made the College Football Playoff.

Two teams have gotten in at 10-3 — Clemson in 2024 and Alabama in 2025 — but both played in their conference championship games. That extra data point matters. A 9-3 team only plays 12 games and doesn't get the benefit of a 13th against another strong opponent in a title game.

Recent near-misses drive the point home. In 2024, Alabama sat at 9-3 and was the first team left out when 11-2 SMU got in. In 2025, Texas finished 9-3 and was the third team on the outside looking in. Those examples show that while the door isn't completely closed, it's a very narrow one.

The current playoff format makes it even tougher, with the new rules in place this season. Now, all four Power conference champions receive automatic bids, and Notre Dame gets an automatic berth if it finishes in the top 12 of the final CFP rankings. That setup locks in several spots and leaves fewer at-large opportunities for three-loss teams, no matter how impressive their résumés look on paper.

Finebaum isn't wrong that Oklahoma's schedule gives it a better shot than most. Games against Michigan, Georgia, Texas and the rest of a brutal SEC gauntlet create the kind of résumé strength the committee has historically rewarded. A couple of those wins, especially on the road or against ranked teams, would carry significant weight. But relying on a 9-3 finish still feels like playing with fire.

The more realistic and healthier goal for this team is 10-2 or better. A 10-2 record with Oklahoma's schedule would essentially lock up a playoff spot. That should be the standard.

The pieces are there for it — a healthy John Mateer, a loaded defense, and more experience across the roster than Brent Venables has had in previous seasons. The early stretch with Michigan, Georgia and Texas will go a long way toward deciding whether that 10-win threshold is reachable.

Finebaum's comment is fair in the sense that the door isn't completely shut at 9-3 for a team with this kind of schedule.

It's just a door that almost never opens.

Oklahoma is better off treating three losses as a worst-case scenario rather than a viable backup plan. Win the games they're supposed to win, take care of business in the middle of the league slate, and put themselves in position where the committee doesn't have to debate them.

The Sooners have already shown they can compete at a high level in the SEC. Last year's playoff appearance proved that. The next step is consistency and finishing with a record that removes any doubt.

Finebaum giving them a path at 9-3 is interesting. Making sure they don't need that path is the better approach.

title: Nick Suzuki Ranked Above Auston Matthews in New NHL Center Rankings
description: A new ranking places the Canadiens captain ahead of Toronto's star in a surprising shakeup.
fullText:
The 2025-26 season proved to be a defining chapter in the career of Nick Suzuki. Montreal's captain reached milestones that only a select few players ever achieve, and the hockey world is finally starting to give him the credit he deserves. A recently released ranking from The Hockey News has now put an official stamp on what many fans in Montreal have believed for some time.

Suzuki posted 29 goals and 101 points during the 2025-26 campaign, crossing the coveted 100-point threshold and firmly establishing himself among the NHL's elite playmakers. On top of that offensive explosion, he took home the Selke Trophy as the league's best defensive forward, a recognition that speaks volumes about his two-way game and his commitment to every aspect of hockey.

The 14th jersey in Montreal carried enormous weight this past season. Suzuki served as the anchor of the top line for what was the second-youngest roster in the entire NHL. Despite the team's youth, his leadership helped guide the Canadiens all the way to the Eastern Conference Finals, a remarkable achievement for a franchise still in its rebuilding phase.

When The Hockey News compiled its list of the top three centers in the Atlantic Division, Suzuki landed at number two. The only player ranked above him was Florida Panthers star Aleksander Barkov. While the Finnish center has never reached the 100-point mark in a single season, his resume featuring two Stanley Cup championships and three Selke Trophies gives him an edge that is hard to argue against.

Perhaps the most striking takeaway from the ranking is the placement of Auston Matthews. The Toronto Maple Leafs captain, long considered one of the most dangerous offensive weapons in the sport, was slotted behind Suzuki at third in the division. His last two seasons have fallen well short of the standards he set earlier in his career, and that decline carried significant weight in the evaluation.

At his peak, Matthews likely still surpasses Suzuki in terms of pure offensive firepower. However, it has been quite some time since the Leafs star performed at the level he displayed in 2023-24, when he lit the lamp 69 times and finished third in Selke Trophy voting.

For Suzuki, this ranking represents something larger than a spot on a list. It signals a shift in perception across the league. He is no longer viewed simply as a promising player on a rebuilding team but rather as one of the premier centers in all of professional hockey. With the Canadiens' young core continuing to develop around him, the trajectory suggests even bigger things could be on the horizon for Montreal's captain.

title: New Michigan basketball coach Mike Boynton is married to former West Ottawa star athlete Jenny Hill
description: Don't be surprised if you see Michigan's new head basketball coach around West Michigan. His wife is from Holland and was a star athlete at WO.
fullText:
GRAND RAPIDS - Jenny Boynton was at her parents' house in Holland last month when she got some big news.

Her husband, Mike Boynton Jr., was just named head coach of the University of Michigan basketball team.

"I love it," she said. "We joked when this became a possibility … I started wearing blue around the house to hint that this is where we needed to be.'"

Boynton - whose maiden name is Jenny Hill - graduated from West Ottawa High School in 2000. She played volleyball and basketball for the Panthers. She would go on to play volleyball at Virginia Tech.

"Just through college athletics," Mike Boynton said. "She was a dietician and I was the head assistant coach at the University of South Carolina back in 2008."

Mike Boynton would eventually become head coach at Oklahoma State University for seven years before taking a job as assistant coach at Michigan last year under Dusty May. The Wolverines won the National Championship and May left to coach in the NBA. So that left the door open for Boynton.

The Boyntons were Grand Rapids on Sunday to watch their son, Ace, play basketball at the Bank Hoops Underclassman All-State Camp. Ace will be an eighth grader this fall.

"I've been to Grand Rapids several times," he said. "My wife is from Holland. We fly into Grand Rapids to see her parents (Brian and Nancy Hill)."

One of Jenny Boynton's good friends is Kristen Redell, the wife of West Ottawa basketball coach Jared Redell. They were all at West Ottawa around the same time.

"I was a few years behind guys like (football player) Rob Renes and (basketball player) Jared Redell," she said. "They were a few years older than me, but they were big names when I was there."

One of the first people she called when she got the news was Kristen Redell. The two were teammates on the volleyball team at West Ottawa.

"Jenny was at her parents house in Holland when they found out that Mike got the job," Redell said. "When they came to Holland recently, we got them into the gym at West Ottawa so the boys could get shots up. Our sons are the same age."

Redell said she her family has always been fans of Michigan basketball.

"Its amazing," she said. "We love Michigan (basketball). We were excited that Mike got the position. It is an amazing tie to West Michigan and the Holland community."

The Boyton's will be back in West Michigan in October. The University of Michigan will play an exhibition on Oct. 25 against the University of Houston at Van Andel Arena.

title: Packers claim former HS All-American receiver Chris Hilton
description: Chris Hilton was a combine invite in 2026 and participated in four pre-draft all-star games
fullText:
The Green Bay Packers worked out multiple receivers today and re-signed receiver Kisean Johnson after a tryout, following short-term injuries to receivers Matthew Golden and Jayden Reed. When the Packers announced their transactions after practice Sunday, which Johnson participated in, it was news that Green Bay waived two players, not one, while adding Johnson, giving the team an open roster spot on the 91-man roster. The players waived were cornerback Marlon Jones and safety Johnathan Baldwin, who both were given injury designations. They will revert to the Packers' injured reserve if they pass through waivers unclaimed. From there, Green Bay can decide whether to end their seasons by keeping them on the injured reserve or pay them out an injury settlement, which would make them free agents while they are rehabbing their injuries.

As I mentioned in The Feed when the news dropped that the Packers had an extra roster spot to fill, this seemed like a move that a team would make before they claimed someone on waivers themselves. It turns out that I was on the right path, as Green Bay was awarded another receiver, Chris Hilton Jr., off waivers today. He should make his Packers debut in Monday's practice, which is open to the public.

Hilton played five years at LSU before going undrafted in the 2026 class, despite participating in four different all-star games (Hula Bowl, American Bowl, East-West Shrine Bowl and Senior Bowl) and receiving a combine invite. At the combine this year, he measured in at 6'0"-flat and 188 pounds and recorded a 4.41-second 40-yard dash.

The former high school All-American had 41 receptions for 780 yards and six touchdowns in his SEC career, but only registered 10 receptions for 122 yards as a redshirt senior, as the Tigers struggled in the passing game after quarterback Garrett Nussmeier injured his abs, which severely limited his play. Nussmeier, who had some first-round hype coming into the 2025 season, wound up going undrafted and signing with the Kansas City Chiefs this spring.

Chris Hilton has okay size for a WR and good speed. Explsoveness is neither a strength nor a weakness, but at his size those poor agility drills are likely to show up when facing NFL cornerbacks. Some things to work with, but some concerns. pic.twitter.com/GZ69HsueAG

Hilton began his NFL career with the Washington Commanders, but he was let go yesterday, a day after the team signed receiver Stefon Diggs to a one-year, $12 million contract.

When Hilton signed with Washington, he received $15,000 in guarantees, which was equal to or more than 6 of the Packers' 11 initial UDFA signings this year:

TE RJ Maryland (waived with an injury designation)

CB Marlon Jones (waived with an injury designation)

Commanders signed Chris Hilton Jr from LSU. I coached him in the Hula Bowl. Kid can play! Nice pickup

Hilton was The Athletic's Dane Brugler's 50th-ranked receiver in the 2026 draft class and received a free agent grade from the draft analyst. Here's his blurb on Hilton:

Christopher "Chris" Hilton Jr. grew up north of Baton Rouge, La., with his parents (Chris Sr. and Cindy), who were both track athletes at Southern University. Hilton was a standout football and track star at Zachary High, where he won several state titles in sprints and jumps (personal best of 10.85 seconds in the 100-meter dash).

A four-star recruit, he was the top-ranked receiver in LSU's 2021 class (ahead of Malik Nabers and Brian Thomas Jr.). Multiple injuries sidetracked his early career, however, as he struggled to find a consistent role beyond being a deep threat.

Hilton looks like a sprinter with his slender, lean-muscled frame and uses his speed to stretch the field. A limited snap count hindered his ability to develop as a route runner, and he was also up and down with his hands — his success rate nosedived when defenders crowded his air space. He has limited return experience but played more on special teams in 2025.

For what it's worth, the injuries he suffered in his career were:

2021 (redshirt season after playing four games): torn meniscus

2022: missed 10 games with shoulder surgery and a torn meniscus in his other knee

2024: missed 7 games with a hairline fracture

In total, he started seven games for the Tigers over five years. His only return experience was as a kick returner during his true freshman and redshirt freshman seasons, when he returned two attempts for a total of 26 yards.

The Packers also reported worked out Devin Voisin, a UDFA who was second-team All-Sun Belt with South Alabama last year, so it's clear that the team was trying to add bodies to the receiver position this week. Voisin has yet to sign with an NFL team, despite being on the Senior Bowl roster this offseason. He was invited to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' rookie minicamp and has also worked out with the Tennessee Titans and Denver Broncos in the last two weeks.

title: Scott Gomez Has Completely Erased Montreal From His Life
description: The former NHLer refuses all contact with anything related to the Canadiens. The story behind his silence is painful.
fullText:
Some stints in professional hockey end quietly, with a player simply moving on to the next chapter. Others leave wounds so deep that they reshape a person's relationship with an entire city. For Scott Gomez, his time with the Montreal Canadiens falls squarely into the latter category, and the extent of the damage has only recently come to light in striking detail.

Journalist Richard Labbé shared a revealing anecdote on BPM Sports that illustrates just how thoroughly Gomez has severed ties with everything connected to the Canadiens organization and the city of Montreal. Labbé recounted how he attempted to set up a Zoom interview with Gomez through the NHL Network. Initially, things seemed promising, and the interview was confirmed. But roughly an hour later, the call came back with a firm and final answer: it was not going to happen. Gomez does not discuss Montreal. He does not want to discuss Montreal. He will not entertain any request that has anything to do with the Quebec metropolis.

The roots of Gomez's total estrangement trace back to one of the most infamous scoring droughts in modern NHL history. The American forward went an entire year without finding the back of the net while wearing the Canadiens jersey. What began as a frustrating slump quickly spiraled into something far more damaging: a full-blown spectacle of public ridicule.

The internet seized on his struggles with merciless creativity. Fans launched so-called "Loto-Gomez" websites where people could wager on when he would finally score his next goal. Inside the Bell Centre, the atmosphere became even more humiliating. Every time Gomez touched the puck, the crowd would erupt in sarcastic applause. Fans stood up and cheered mockingly. Some supporters even showed up wearing sombreros in the stands, turning each game into a carnival of derision directed at a single player.

According to Labbé, this episode stands out as one of the rare instances in professional hockey where a player became a public laughingstock in real time, right on the ice surface where he was trying to do his job. The cruelty of that treatment, sustained over months, appears to have left an indelible mark on Gomez.

While many athletes eventually find a way to look back on difficult chapters with some distance or even humor, Gomez has clearly chosen a different path. The fact that years after leaving the organization he still refuses any conversation remotely connected to Montreal speaks to the depth of the psychological toll. For a player who had enjoyed a successful career that included a Stanley Cup and significant contracts, the Montreal chapter remains a wound he has no interest in reopening. Whether time will ever soften that stance remains to be seen, but for now, the name Montreal is entirely off limits in Scott Gomez's world.

title: Hagen Smith, Colson Montgomery Lead White Sox to Series Win Over Guardians
description: Hagen Smith delivered two scoreless innings in his MLB debut, while Colson Montgomery’s three-run homer lifted the White Sox to a crucial series win.
fullText:
It will be the division games that matter most for the Chicago White Sox down the stretch of the 2026 season. And after suffering another difficult-to-stomach sweep at the hands of the Boston Red Sox, the White Sox answered with a big weekend series win over the Cleveland Guardians.

It all came down to Sunday's rubber match, when Davis Martin took the ball and surrendered two runs in the first inning before being removed from the game following a rain delay that lasted more than two hours.

The early stages of the game did not set up well for Chicago. While the offense jumped on Joey Cantillo with three consecutive hits to start the game, the White Sox left two runners in scoring position with nobody out in the bottom of the first inning. They then immediately went into the rain delay trailing 2-1, knowing their starting pitcher would be done for the day after recording just three outs.

That was a big blow for a White Sox team with an already taxed bullpen, one that had been pushed to the limit Thursday night in Boston during a 13-inning defeat. But with a key off day coming Monday, manager Will Venable emptied the tank, and the White Sox relievers proved up to the task. That included left-handed pitcher Hagen Smith, the No. 2 prospect in the White Sox organization, who made his MLB debut Sunday.

Smith's debut was true to form. He recorded his first MLB strikeout on three pitches against Brayan Rocchio, the first batter he faced. He struck out the side in his first inning of work, even managing to punch out the notoriously stingy Steven Kwan.

Smith's second inning, however, was much tougher. He walked three batters to load the bases with two outs, then worked a full count against Rocchio before inducing a lineout to third baseman Miguel Vargas. Smith escaped the jam despite issuing four walks on the day, ultimately throwing two scoreless innings and earning the win in his first MLB appearance.

He got that win thanks to Colson Montgomery, who stepped up with two runners on and two outs in the bottom of the third inning and pummeled a Craig Yoho pitch 110.7 mph for his 26th home run of the year. That blast put the White Sox on top 5-2, a lead they held for the rest of the afternoon.

The Colson Montgomery haters are in SHAMBLES!#WhiteSox lead 5-2 on his 26th home run. pic.twitter.com/zz9rq3tqqt

It was an impressive display by the White Sox, who picked themselves up off the mat following a rough start to the game. Both the offense and the pitching staff did enough to secure the win.

"We all stayed pretty much locked in," Montgomery said of the rain delay during his postgame interview with Brooke Fletcher. "We treated it like a whole new ballgame, 0-0."

That win gives the White Sox their largest division lead of the season. It also put a new team in Chicago's rearview mirror. The White Sox now hold a 3.5 game lead in the AL Central, and it is the red-hot Detroit Tigers who sit in second place, with Cleveland and Minnesota both 4.0 games back.

The Tigers are 7-2 over their last nine games. It's an ironic time for a hot streak after they traded both Tarik Skubal and Casey Mize at the MLB trade deadline, but they are by no means out of the race. The White Sox will have to keep taking care of business and stacking series wins if they want to run away with the AL Central crown.

A series win over the Guardians was a good start, but the difficult tests are not over. Next weekend, the White Sox will travel to Detroit for a three-game series against the Tigers.

title: Former Eagles draft pick returns for free-agent tryout
description: The Eagles hosted David Blay, Ja’Quinden Jackson and former draft pick Tarron Jackson as they evaluate depth at three positions
fullText:
The Philadelphia Eagles aren't waiting until the preseason opener to evaluate potential roster additions. According to the NFL transaction wire, Philadelphia hosted defensive tackle David Blay, running back Ja'Quinden Jackson, and linebacker Tarron Jackson for free-agent visits Sunday.

Workouts and visits don't guarantee a signing. Teams routinely evaluate available players during training camp to ensure they have up-to-date medical information and a list of potential replacements in case of injuries.

Still, Philadelphia's three visitors are worth examining. Blay is a local product coming off his final season at Miami. Ja'Quinden Jackson offers size and power at running back, while Tarron Jackson is a familiar face after beginning his NFL career with the Eagles.

Blay may be the most intriguing developmental prospect of the three. The Levittown, Pennsylvania, native signed with New England as an undrafted rookie after playing at West Chester, Louisiana Tech and Miami. The Patriots released him Friday, allowing Philadelphia to bring him in two days later. New England lists Blay at 6-foot-2 and 292 pounds. He played 46 games during his college career, finishing with 129 tackles, 11.5 sacks, one forced fumble and one pass breakup. He recorded 28 tackles during his final season at Miami. The Patriots signed him May 8 before releasing him Aug. 7.

Blay's most productive season came at Louisiana Tech in 2024. He recorded 46 tackles, 10.5 tackles for loss and 6.5 sacks while earning first-team All-Conference USA honors. Philadelphia already has Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo and Byron Young occupying prominent places in the defensive tackle rotation. Gabe Hall is among the players competing for a reserve role. That makes Blay more of a developmental option than someone likely to earn immediate playing time.

His local ties, college production and recent availability make him a logical player to evaluate. Of the three visitors, Blay may have the clearest chance to receive a contract if the Eagles want another interior defender for the remainder of camp.

Jackson entered college as a quarterback before eventually moving to running back at Utah. His most productive season came after transferring to Arkansas. The 6-foot-2, 233-pound runner carried the ball 149 times for 790 yards and 15 touchdowns in 2024. He also caught 13 passes for 139 yards, displaying more receiving ability than his bruising frame might suggest.

Jackson signed with Jacksonville as an undrafted rookie in 2025. He carried 13 times for 56 yards and caught two passes for 13 yards during the preseason but didn't make the initial roster. He later returned to the Jaguars' practice squad and signed a reserve/futures deal before Jacksonville waived him May 11.

The Eagles already have Saquon Barkley leading a backfield that includes Tank Bigsby and Dameon Pierce. ShunDerrick Powell is also seeking a role. That makes an immediate signing less likely unless Philadelphia is dealing with an undisclosed injury or wants another runner to absorb preseason carries.

Jackson's power would give the Eagles another short-yardage option, but his path to the roster would be difficult.

Tarron Jackson requires little introduction inside the Jefferson Health Training Complex. Philadelphia selected him with the 191st overall pick in the sixth round of the 2021 NFL Draft. Jackson appeared in 21 games over his first two seasons with the Eagles. His lone NFL sack came against the Detroit Lions during his rookie year. He later spent time with Carolina before returning to Philadelphia's practice squad in 2024.

Across 24 career games with the Eagles and Panthers, Jackson has recorded 17 tackles, one sack and one forced fumble. Philadelphia originally drafted him after he produced 195 tackles, 44.5 tackles for loss and 26.5 sacks at Coastal Carolina. Jackson joined San Francisco in 2025 but landed on injured reserve after suffering a neck injury during training camp. His visit allows the Eagles to evaluate his health while determining whether he can provide useful depth at outside linebacker.

Philadelphia has several edge defenders ahead of him, including Jalyx Hunt, Jonathan Greenard, Nolan Smith, Arnold Ebiketie and A.J. Epenesa. Jackson's familiarity with the organization could still work in his favor if the Eagles need another experienced practice body or special teams contributor.

The Eagles don't have an obvious need to sign any of the three immediately. Blay offers developmental upside, Ja'Quinden Jackson provides power at running back, and Tarron Jackson brings familiarity.

Philadelphia may simply be updating its emergency list. If a signing follows, Blay's youth and interior pass-rush production make him the most logical candidate. At the same time, Tarron Jackson would offer the easiest transition because of his previous experience with the organization.

title: Vollering wins Tour de France Femmes after war of nerves
description: Dutch rider Demi Vollering took the Tour de France Femmes overall title in style on Sunday, winning the hilly final stage to extend her lead on nearest rival Kasia Niewiadoma, who finished second overall after a tense struggle.The 29-year-old also won the 2023 title and earned her second one by timing the nine-day slog to perfection, carving out solo wins on the final two stages, which both ended in Nice.
fullText:
Dutch rider Demi Vollering took the Tour de France Femmes overall title in style on Sunday, winning the hilly final stage to extend her lead on nearest rival Kasia Niewiadoma, who finished second overall after a tense struggle.

The 29-year-old also won the 2023 title and earned her second one by timing the nine-day slog to perfection, carving out solo wins on the final two stages, which both ended in Nice.

"It's a dream to live this life," Vollering said after hoisting her bike above her head at the finish line.

"I knew my level and even when Kasia won on Mont Ventoux I was still confident," added Vollering, who has also finished second on this race three times in its five editions since being relaunched in 2022.

Vollering's FDJ-United Suez are the first French team to win the race, earning her high praise from team boss Stephen Delcourt.

"Through her high standards, sensitivity, authenticity, and the way she brings others along with her, she is redefining what it means to be a modern leader," he said.

"She inspires her teammates, she inspires the fans, she inspires an entire generation ... She doesn't just win races; she shows the way forward."

Vollering had to carve out this win.

Niewiadoma took the yellow jersey on Friday's climb of Mont Ventoux, setting up a pulsating finale.

Vollering then edged into the overall lead on Saturday, attacking late on a small hill and edging into an eight-second overall advantage over 2024 winner Niewiadoma.

A furious Niewiadoma, however, complained she had been blocked by a teammate of Vollering's at a crucial moment, but no action was taken.

Vollering said her team had been both "honest and humble" after Sunday's race, adding that her teammate Celia Gery, the alleged blocker, had received death threats on social media.

"Celia had a really bad night. I'm sure deep down that Kasia knows these kind of things can happen in a race," Vollering said.

The scene was set for a dramatic final stage contested over four climbs of the Col d'Eze just outside Nice, where Vollering waited until the fourth ascent to pounce.

Attacking near the summit, she took a 20sec lead and thundered down towards Nice, never looking back.

Italy's Elisa Longo Borghini came third overall after Swiss rider Marlen Reusser fell on a descent and lost a two-minute cushion on the podium.

Dutch sprinter Lorena Wiebes won the green sprint points jersey mainly thanks to her victories on the two opening stages in Switzerland.

Her compatriot Puck Pieterse secured the polka dot climb jersey ahead of the final stage.

The best young rider jersey was won by Germany's Antonia Niedermaier, who also finished fourth overall.

title: Orioles’ Pete Alonso gets real about backing up talk after big game vs. Rangers
description: Baltimore Orioles slugger Pete Alonso had a big day against the Texas Rangers in a much needed win for his ballclub.
fullText:
Orioles' Pete Alonso gets real about backing up talk after big game vs. Rangers appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

The Baltimore Orioles needed a win over the Texas Rangers on Sunday in the worst way. Baltimore had lost five of their last seven games. If they wanted to stay in the race for the AL Wild Card, a victory on Sunday was essential. Thankfully, veteran slugger Pete Alonso came through.

Alonso strode to the plate five times against Texas, reaching safely in every plate appearance. He walked twice, swatted two home runs, and drove in four runs. Baltimore won 10-5, and that performance was a vital one for Alonso, as he explained after the game.

"You can't talk and be vocal if you're not doing it. For me, you've got to do it, and then you talk afterwards whenever there's time. But also, in order to be a leader, who have to have done it and continuously be doing it," the Orioles star said, via Andy Kostka of Diamondback Sports.
